ety: Borrowed from French illégal, from Medieval Latin illegalis, from Latin legalis, by surface analysis, il- + legal. In senses relating to immigration, via clipping of illegal alien or illegal immigrant.

s.def: Contrary to, forbidden, or not authorized by law, especially criminal law.
ex: This is illegal, you know!
Nearly 40 million people live in UK areas with illegal air pollution
It's illegal to go over 70mph on any British road, so why should drivers have cars that can?

s.def: Forbidden by established rules.
ex: Moving a pawn backward is an illegal move in chess.
The computer program performed an illegal operation and was terminated.

s.def: Totally fictitious, and often issued on behalf of a non-existent territory or country.
Being or doing something illegally.
ex: illegal immigrant
illegal logger
illegal pilot

s.def: Being an illegal immigrant; residing in a country illegally.
An illegal act or technique.
Contraband, esp. illegal substances such as drugs.
ex: …I've got illegals in my bottom…!

s.def: A spy operating abroad illegally and under non-official cover, without visible ties to his or her country’s authorities.
Ellipsis of illegal immigrant.
The characteristic or quality of being illegible; the quality of being difficult or impossible to read.
ex: The illegibility of his handwriting made it unclear which answer he wrote.
I passed the time by adding to the illegibilities in my diary.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English il- English legible English illegible From il- + legible.

ex: illegible handwriting
illegible scribbles
illegible symbols

ety: First attested in 1536, from Latin illēgitimus, most likely an adapted borrowing of Middle French illegitime, equivalent to il- + legitimate, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

s.def: Not in accordance with the law.
Not sanctioned by marriage.
ex: If we credit the scandal of the former [i.e. his enemies], Artaxerxes sprang from the illegitimate commerce of a tanner’s wife with a common soldier.
His illegitimate birth deprived him of the influence of a father until perhaps his fifth year […]

s.def: Not conforming to known principles, or established or accepted rules or standards.
ex: […] it may be impossible to convince them that the illegitimate power which they obtain, by degrading themselves, is a curse […]

s.def: Not correctly deduced.
ex: an illegitimate inference

s.def: Not authorized by good usage; not genuine.
ex: an illegitimate word

s.def: Involving the fertilization of pistils by stamens not of their own length, in heterogonously dimorphic and trimorphic flowers.
ex: illegitimate union; illegitimate fertilization

s.def: A person born to unmarried parents.
ex: Her father and mine was a shameless man and of all his illegitimates I am the most unfortunate and poverty stricken.

s.def: To make illegitimate.

ety: From Middle French illibéral, from Latin illiberalis, equivalent to il- + liberal.

s.def: Restricting or failing to sufficiently promote individual choice and freedom.
Narrow-minded; bigoted.
ex: While they maintained a denominational character, they were in nowise illiberal, and set up no religious test for entrance.

s.def: Ungenerous, stingy.
Not adhering to either liberalism or neoliberalism.
One opposed to liberal principles.

ety: Borrowed from French illicite, from Latin illicitus, from in- (“not”) + licitus (“allowed, permitted”), from licet (“it is allowed”). By surface analysis, il- + licit.

s.def: Not approved by law, but not invalid.
ex: The bigamous marriage, while illicit, was not invalid.
Such migrants may violate our laws against illicit entry, but if that's all they do then they are trespassers, not criminals.

s.def: Breaking social norms.
ex: I only can properly enjoy carol services if I am having an illicit affair with someone in the congregation.

s.def: Unlawful.
A banned or unlawful item.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English il- English limitable English illimitable From il- + limitable.

s.def: Impervious to limitation, without limit.
ex: Through the sense of touch I know […] the illimitable variety of straight and curved lines,

ety: First attested in 1425–1475, in Middle English; from Middle English illiterat(e) (“uneducated, ignorant of Latin”), borrowed from Latin illīterātus, illitterātus (“unlearned, ignorant”), itself from in- (“un-”) + līterātus, litterātus (“furnished with letters”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from lītera, littera (“letter, character”). The noun was derived from the adjective by substantivization, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

s.def: Unable to read and write.
ex: About half of the population in Ethiopia is illiterate.

s.def: Not conforming to prescribed standards of speech or writing.
Ignorant in a specified way or about a specified subject.
ex: technologically illiterate, economically illiterate, emotionally illiterate

s.def: Having less than an expected standard of familiarity with language and literature, or having little formal education.
ex: He's illiterate […] Seriously, how did he get into RI?

s.def: An illiterate person, one either not able to read and write or not knowing how.
ex: We might also provide education plus reading and writing services to adult illiterates.

s.def: A person ignorant about a given subject. (The relevant subject is usually named as a noun adjunct.)
ex: Their government is run by business illiterates.
Sometimes a mathematical illiterate is called an innumerate.

ety: Etymology tree English ill Proto-Germanic *-in- Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ti Proto-Germanic *-ōną Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English illness From ill + -ness.

s.def: An instance (episode) of a disease or poor health.
ex: Her grandmother had passed away after a long illness.
suffer form a severe illness
a mild illness

s.def: A state of bad health or disease.
ex: Many working days this year have been lost through illness.
Illness is a wholistic reality, just as health is wholistic, and healing is the process of moving from illness to health.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English il- English logical English illogical From il- + logical.

s.def: Contrary to logic; lacking sense or sound reasoning.
ex: I received an illogical reply and that left me standing there feeling confused.
Your highly emotional reaction is most illogical.
'Cause I was feeling so illogical, d-d-d-igital

ety: From Middle English illuminaten, borrowed from Latin illūminātus, perfect passive participle of illūminō (“lighten, light up, show off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from in + lūminō (“light up”), from lūmen (“light”). Cognate with Old English lȳman (“to glow, shine”). More at leam.

s.def: To shine light on something.
ex: A light that is one foot away from the subject's face will completely illuminate the face, but leave the rest of the body softer and darker.

s.def: To decorate something with lights.
To clarify or make something understandable.
ex: The situation, as it was, made it more difficult for him to leave. Yet it illuminated the very reasons why he had to go.

s.def: To decorate the page of a manuscript book with ornamental designs.
To make spectacular.
ex: Hodgson's approach may not illuminate proceedings in Poland and Ukraine but early evidence suggests they will be tough to break down.

s.def: To glow; to light up.
ex: Red diode in button illuminates when camera runs at speed set in five-digit speed selector.
Say my name / and every color illuminates. / We are shining / […]

s.def: To be exposed to light.
To direct a radar beam toward.
Enlightened, illuminated, made bright.
ex: February 28 1630, Joseph Hall, The Hypocrite do ye see an illuminate elder of the anabaptists rapt in divine ecstasies?

s.def: Enlightened spiritually, divinely taught or inspired; in technical use, converted, baptized.

ety: From illuminate + -ing.

s.def: Providing illumination or light.
Providing clarification or explanation; educational, revealing.

s.def: The act of illuminating, or supplying with light; the state of being illuminated.
ex: The room was filled with soft illumination from the candles.
The people hereabouts, sir, would seem to dispense with street illumination, and it is very dark tonight.

s.def: Festive decoration of houses or buildings with lights.
Adornment of books and manuscripts with colored illustrations. See illuminate (transitive verb).
Splendour; brightness.
Enlightening influence; inspiration.
ex: The philosopher’s work gave intellectual illumination to many.

ety: From Middle English illuminen (“to light, light up; to shine; (figuratively) to enlighten spiritually; to make illustrious”) [and other forms], from Old French illuminer (“to light up, illuminate; (figuratively) to enlighten”) (modern French illuminer), from Latin illūmināre, the present active infinitive of illūminō (“to light up, illuminate; to brighten; to adorn; to make conspicuous”), from il- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘in, within’; intensifying prefix)) + lūminō (“to illuminate; to b…

s.def: Synonym of illuminate.
ex: The pages which I have the privilege of now introducing to the world, are calculated, I trust, to illumine the dark parts of the field of morals— […]
I am like a happy lover / Who illumines life with dreaming!
[T]he possibility that illustrations could actually illumine writing and draw out elements of a narrative doesn’t seem to count for much any more.

ety: From Old French illusion, from Latin illūsiō, from illūdere, from in- (“at, upon”) + lūdere (“to play, mock, trick”). Displaced native Old English dwimmer.

s.def: The state of being deceived or misled.
A distortion of sensory perception where real stimuli lead to a false or misleading impression of reality.
ex: We saw what looked like a tiger among the trees, but it was an illusion caused by the shadows of the branches.
Using artificial additives, scientists can create the illusion of fruit flavours in food.
You realize the sun don't go down it's just an illusion caused by the world spinning round.

s.def: A misapprehension; a belief in something that is in fact not true.
ex: Jane has this illusion that John is in love with her.

s.def: A magician’s trick.

ety: Etymology tree English illusion Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-tās Ancient Greek -τής (-tḗs) Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. Latin -istader. Old French -istebor. Middle English -ist English -ist English illusionist From illusion + -ist.

s.def: One who works with illusion or sleight of hand.
One who deceives by magical or mystical means.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin illūsīvus.

s.def: Subject to or pertaining to an illusion, often used in the sense of an unrealistic expectation or an unreachable goal or outcome.
ex: Testing software completely is an illusive goal.
[…] he could not catch the illusive thing that had sadly perplexed as well as elevated his spirit.

ety: Back-formation from illustration.

s.def: To clarify something by giving, or serving as, an example or a comparison.
ex: We illustrate our definitions by including quotations or simple examples.
To prove him, and illustrate his high worth.

s.def: To provide a book or other publication with pictures, diagrams or other explanatory or decorative features.
ex: The economics textbook was illustrated with many graphs.

s.def: To shed light upon.
ex: Here, when the morn illustrates all the sky.

s.def: To give renown or honour to; to make illustrious.
ex: Matter to me of glory, whom their hate / Illustrates.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French illustration, from Latin illūstrātiō, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”). By surface analysis, illustrate + -ion.

s.def: The act of illustrating; the act of making clear and distinct.
Something which illustrates; a comparison or example intended to make clear or apprehensible, or to remove obscurity.
A picture designed to decorate a publication, or elucidate a literary work.
ex: The illustration showing the water cycle made it much easier to understand for the children.
The sleeve of the band's new CD includes illustrations from deceased former members.
Fossils show that the ancient primate Proconsul africanus, shown in the illustration above, was a tailless tree-dweller.

s.def: The state of being illustrated, or of being made clear and distinct.
A calculated prevision of insurance premiums and returns (life insurance).

s.def: Demonstrative, exemplative, showing an example or demonstrating.
ex: This latest incident is illustrative of his continued bad behavior.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Latin lūstrō Latin illūstrō Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin illūstrātiōbor. Middle French illustrationbor. English illustrationbf. English illustrate English -or English illustrator From illustrate + -or.

s.def: a person who draws pictures (especially illustrations in books or magazines)
ex: Mary is one of the best illustrators of children's books in the country.

ety: From Latin illūstris (“bright, shining; distinguished, prominent, illustrious”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, to denote possession or presence of a quality in any degree). Illūstris is derived from illūstrō (“to brighten, illuminate; to make famous or illustrious”), from in- (“in, inside”) + lūstrō (“to purify by making a sacrifice; to brighten, illuminate”) (from lūstrō (“purificatory sacrifice”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”) or *lewh…

s.def: Admired, distinguished, respected, or well-known.

ety: Named after Ilmen Mountains in Russia + -ite in 1827.

s.def: A weakly magnetic dark gray mineral found in metamorphic and igneous rocks; it is a mixed oxide of iron and titanium, FeTiO₃
ex: The basalt of Goose Island of the Ice Harbor Member is unique for the occurrence of microphenocrysts of ilmenite and titanmagnetite.

ety: From Middle English ymage, borrowed from Old French image, from Latin imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym-; the same PIE root is the source of imitari (“to copy, imitate”); see imitate. Doublet of imago.

s.def: A mental picture of something not real or not present.
A file that contains all information needed to produce a live working copy. (See disk image and image copy.)
ex: Most game console emulators do not come with any ROM images for copyright reasons.

s.def: A characteristic of a person, group or company etc., style, manner of dress, how one is or wishes to be perceived by others.
graphical representation
math: something mapped to by a function
To reflect, mirror.
ex: Sorrow was dead indeed in her, but peace and perfect happiness were born; imaged in her tranquil beauty and profound repose.

s.def: To create an image of.
To create a complete backup copy of a file system or other entity.
A visual or other representation of the external form of something in art.
ex: The Bible forbids the worship of graven images.

s.def: A statue or idol.

der: an image is worth a thousand words

ety: From Middle English ymagerie, from Middle French imagerie; equivalent to image + -ry.

s.def: The work of one who makes images or visible representation of objects.
Imitation work.
Images in general, or en masse.
Unreal show; imitation; appearance.
The work of the imagination or fancy; false ideas; imaginary phantasms.
Rhetorical decoration in writing or speaking; vivid descriptions presenting or suggesting images of sensible objects; figures in discourse.

ety: From Middle English ymaginable, from Latin imāginābilis; equivalent to imagine + -able.

s.def: Able to be imagined; conceivable.
ex: While running, they were exposed to the most hideous bespawling imaginable.
By the early 1980s, Gucci was overlicensed, with its logo on every product imaginable from headscarves to key rings to lighters.

ety: From Middle English ymaginarie, ymagynary, from Latin imāginārius (“relating to images, fancied”), from imāgō, equivalent to imagine + -ary. The mathematical sense derives from René Descartes's use (of the French imaginaire) in 1637, La Geometrie, to ridicule the notion of regarding non-real roots of polynomials as numbers. Although Descartes' usage was derogatory, the designation stuck even after the concept gained acceptance in the 18th century.

s.def: Existing only in the imagination.
ex: imaginary friend
Unicorns are imaginary.

s.def: Relating or belonging to the imagination.
ex: Fiction refers to imaginary stories.

s.def: Having no real part; that part of a complex number which is a multiple of √ (called imaginary unit).
Imagination; fancy.
An imaginary number.
The set of values, institutions, laws, and symbols common to a particular social group and the corresponding society through which people imagine their social whole.

ety: The adjective imaginary in this context was first used (as French imaginaire) by René Descartes in 1673, La Geometrie, referring to imaginary numbers in the broad sense, as non-real roots of polynomials. Descartes' usage was derogatory, but the concept later gained acceptance through the work of Leonhard Euler and Carl Friedrich Gauss in the 18th century.

s.def: A number of the form bi, where b is any real number and i denotes the imaginary unit.
A number of the form a + bi, where a and b are real numbers and b is nonzero.

ety: From Middle English ymaginacioun, from Old French imaginacion, ymaginacion, from Latin imāginātiō. Equivalent to imagine + -ation.

s.def: The image-making power of the mind; the act of mentally creating or reproducing an object not previously perceived; the ability to create such images.
ex: Imagination is one of the most advanced human faculties.
She removed Stranleigh’s coat with a dexterity that aroused his imagination.

s.def: A mental image formed by the action of the imagination as a faculty; something imagined.
ex: It is a pleasant imagination to conceive a spirit iustly ballanced betweene two equall desires.
And yet the invention of young men, is more lively than that of old; and imaginations stream into their minds better, and, as it were, more divinely.

s.def: Creativity; resourcefulness.
ex: His imagination makes him a valuable team member.

s.def: Particularly, construction of false images; fantasizing.
ex: You think someone's been following you? That's just your imagination.

der: by any stretch of the imagination
by no stretch of the imagination

ety: From Middle English ymagynatif, from Middle French imaginatif, from Medieval Latin imāginātīvus. By surface analysis, imagine + -ative.

s.def: Having a lively or creative imagination.
ex: an imaginative boy
No doubt kibitzers are highly imaginative. How else could they see wins and brilliant combinations that do not exist?

s.def: Tending to be fanciful or inventive.
ex: an imaginative story

s.def: False or imagined.

ety: From Middle English ymagynen, from Middle French imaginer, from Latin imāginor, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

s.def: To form a mental image of something; to envision or create something in one's mind.
ex: Try to imagine a pink elephant.
Imagine yourself in a packed airport lounge.
Imagine sitting on a tropical beach with a cool mimosa.

s.def: To believe in something created by one's own mind, often something false.
ex: She imagined that the man wanted to kill her.
There's nothing there; you're just imagining things.

s.def: To assume; to suppose.
ex: I imagine that he will need to rest after such a long flight.

s.def: To conjecture; to guess.
ex: I cannot even imagine what you are up to!
The board imagines the merger will increase profits by 25%

s.def: To use one's imagination.
ex: Imagine that we were siblings.

s.def: To contrive in purpose; to scheme; to devise.
Used to mock an idea by suggesting that it is ridiculous or ill thought through.
ex: Imagine thinking that would work.

s.def: A short fanfic or prompt placing a reader insert in a novel scenario with a character or celebrity.
ex: Some imagines are more sexual and creepy than others: "Imagine Stiles walking in on you giving Scott a blowjob."
i personally like imagines and fanfics so i found a good amount of kylo ren x reader fics and started going through them.
If I get inspired immediately, I can bust out an imagine in 5-10 minutes.

ety: From Latin imāgō. Doublet of image. Compare typologically a Russian term for coordinate larva: личи́нка (ličínka) (akin to лик (lik)).

s.def: The final developmental stage of an insect after undergoing metamorphosis.
An idealised concept of a loved one, formed in childhood and retained unconsciously into adult life, the basis for the psychological formation of personality archetypes.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic إِمَام (ʔimām, “leader”).

s.def: Muslim leader
One who leads the salat prayers in a mosque.
ex: Sheik Mohammad Seyed Tantawi, Egypt’s highest-ranking imam, led the prayers over the coffin, covered with an Egyptian flag.

s.def: A Shi'ite Muslim leader descended from the prophet Muhammad and functioning as his spiritual successor.

ety: From imam + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

s.def: The office or jurisdiction of an imam.
ex: The government has accused the Houthis of trying to restore the traditional Zaidi-led imamate that largely ruled Yemen until 1962.

ety: From Ottoman Turkish عمارت (ʼimaret), from Arabic عِمَارَة (ʕimāra).

s.def: An Ottoman soup kitchen built between the fourteenth and nineteenth centuries, often part of a larger complex or waqf.
ex: He lived in an elegant stone house, a part of the Imaret of Haseki Sultan.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English im- Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Italic *dwi- Latin bi- Latin lanx Latin bilanx Vulgar Latin *bilancia Old French balancebor. Middle English balaunce English balance English imbalance From im- + balance.

s.def: The property of not being in balance.
ex: The growing imbalances between the rich and poor first lead to more crime.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French imbécile, from Latin imbēcillus (“weak, feeble”), literally “without a staff”.

s.def: A person with limited mental capacity who can perform tasks and think only like a young child, in medical circles meaning a person who lacks the capacity to develop beyond the mental age of a normal five- to seven-year-old child.
ex: It is an offence for a man to have unlawful sexual intercourse with a woman whom he knows to be an idiot or imbecile.

s.def: A fool, an idiot.
ex: VLADIMIR: Because he wouldn't save them. / ESTRAGON: From hell? / VLADIMIR: Imbecile! From death.

s.def: Destitute of strength, whether of body or mind; feeble; impotent; especially, mentally weak.
ex: hospitals for the imbecile and insane
And then that imbecile crowd down on the deck started their little fun, and I could see nothing more for smoke.

ety: From Middle English inbecillite, from Middle French imbecilité, imbecillité, and its etymon Classical Latin imbēcillitās. By surface analysis, imbecile + -ity.

s.def: The quality of being imbecile; weakness; feebleness, especially of mind.
Something imbecilic; a stupid action, behaviour, etc.
ex: The Parnassian theory of art is mere imbecility.
The procedure of musical comedy is not reducible to a coherent formula, so that its imbecilities may be annotated by super imbecilities.

ety: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.

s.def: To drink (used frequently of alcoholic beverages).
ex: Without its sting, the common yellowjacket would be unable to steal ham from our sandwich or imbibe the sweet juice from our peach.

s.def: To take in; absorb.
ex: to imbibe knowledge

s.def: To steep; to cause to absorb liquid.

ety: Borrowed from Latin imbricātus (“tiled”).

s.def: Alternative form of imbricated (“overlapping”).
To overlap in a regular pattern.
To undergo or cause to undergo imbrication.

ety: Participle adjective, imbricate + -ed.

s.def: Overlapping, like scales or roof-tiles; intertwined.

ety: Borrowed from Italian imbroglio (“tangle, entanglement, muddle”) (im-, alternative form of in- (prefix forming verbs denoting derivation) + broglio (“confusion; intrigue, fraud, rigging, stuffing”); see also imbrogliare (“to tangle”)), cognate with and probably from an earlier form of French embrouiller (“to embroil, muddle”) (em- (“em-”), a form of en- (“en-”, prefix meaning ‘caused’) + brouiller (“to confuse, mix up”)). Doublet of embroil.

s.def: A complicated situation; an entanglement.
ex: Into the drawers and china pry, / Papers and books, a huge imbroglio! / Under a tea-cup he might lie, / Or creased, like dogs-ears, in a folio.

ety: From Middle English embrewen, from Old French *embrever (whence Middle French embreuver), metathetic variant of embevrer (“to imbibe, steep, penetrate, soak”) (with same stem variation found in French abreuver and beuverie), from Vulgar Latin imbiberāre.

s.def: To stain [with in or with ‘blood, slaughter, etc.’].
ex: My hands were imbrued in his blood.

ety: From im- + brute. Akin to Italian imbruttire, Spanish embrutecer, Catalan embrutar.

s.def: To make brutal
To degrade to the state of a brute
ex: How deep was the change, made upon the imbruted Asiatics, we may perhaps question.
Notwithstanding all that has been said, the solitary is a man imbruted, vegetating, deprived of his crown.

ety: From Latin imbuō (“wet, moisten”). Compare imbibe.

s.def: To instill or inspire (someone) with a certain quality, feeling, or idea.
To wet or stain an object completely with some physical quality.
ex: The shirt was imbued with his scent.

s.def: In general, to act in a way which results in an object becoming completely permeated or impregnated by some quality.
ex: The entire text is imbued with the sense of melancholy and hopelessness.

ety: From French imitable, from Latin imitābilis. See imitate.

s.def: Capable of being imitated or copied.
ex: The characters of man placed in lower stations of life are more usefull, as being imitable by great numbers.

s.def: Worthy of imitation.

ety: Borrowed from Latin imitātus, perfect active participle of imitor (“to copy, portray, imitate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French imiter.

s.def: To follow as a model or a pattern; to make a copy, counterpart or semblance of.
ex: A wave simulator in the tank can re-enact tsunamis and northeasters, and imitate wave conditions from midocean.
The room was dark and cool, lit with a dim red light. “This was designed to imitate a cave,” said Rosas.

ety: From Middle English imitacioun, from Middle French imitacion, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitatio.

s.def: The act of imitating.

ety: From im- + pecunious, from Latin pecūniōsus, from pecūnia (“money”) + -ōsus (“full of”).

ety: From impede + -ance. In sense 2 and sense 3 it was coined by English mathematician and physicist Oliver Heaviside in 1886.

ety: Borrowed from Latin impediō (“to shackle”), from pēs (“foot”) (compare pedestrian). First attested use as a verb was in William Shakespeare's Macbeth, see quotations.

ety: From Middle English impediment, borrowed from Latin impedimentum.

ety: From Middle English impellen, borrowed from Latin impellō.

ety: Borrowed from Latin impendere (“to hang over, to weigh out”), 1590s.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English im- English plausible English implausible From im- + plausible.

ex: Harper finds the idea that Latin developed into the modern Romance languages too implausible to believe.

ety: From im- + pledge.

s.def: To pledge.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).

s.def: bring about
To bring about; to put into practice; to carry out.
ex: Near-synonyms: realize, actualize, materialize; embody; accomplish
It’s a good thought, but it will be a difficult thing to implement.

s.def: A tool or instrument for working with.
ex: farming implements
agricultural implements
They carried an assortment of gardening implements in the truck.

ety: From implement + -ation.

s.def: The process of moving an idea from concept to reality. In business, engineering and other fields, implementation refers to the building process rather than the design process.
ex: Now that the requirements are complete we can move on to implementation.

s.def: A result of implementing something; a finished product, system or device.
ex: His implementation works, but it needs some fine-tuning.

ety: From implement + -er.

s.def: A person who implements something.

ety: From Late Latin implētiō (past participle of Latin impleō (“to fill up”) + -iō); see also implement.

s.def: An act of filling; the state of being full.
A substance which fills, a filling.

ety: First attested in the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicaten (poorly attested), from implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined; involved, connected (with)”, possibly also used as the past participle of implicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin implicātus, perfect passive participle of implicō (“to entangle, involve”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from plicō (“to fold”). Doublet of imply and employ.

s.def: To show to be connected or involved in an unfavorable or criminal way.
ex: The evidence implicates involvement of top management in the scheme.
I shall cancel, without further provocation, the next lecture engagement that is implicated with a peep o' day train.

s.def: To imply, to have as a necessary consequence or accompaniment.
ex: What did Nixon's visit to China implicate for Russia?

s.def: To imply without entailing; to have as an implicature.
To fold or twist together, intertwine, interlace, entangle, entwine.
The thing implied.
Intertwined, enfolded, twisted together; wrapped up (with), entangled, involved (in).
Involved, intricate.

English implication From Middle French implication, from Latin implicationem (accusative of implicatio). Equivalent to implicate + -ion.

s.def: An implying, or that which is implied, but not expressed; an inference, or something which may fairly be understood, though not expressed in words.
The connective in propositional calculus that, when joining two predicates A and B in that order, has the meaning "if A is true, then B is true".
The act of implicating.
The state of being implicated.
A possible, or indirect, effect or result of a decision or action.
ex: Dumping waste in the river will have serious implications for the environment.

s.def: Logical consequence.

ety: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.

s.def: Suggested indirectly, without being directly expressed; Implied.
ex: Poets often leave behind an implicit message within their words.

s.def: Contained in the essential nature of something but not openly shown.
Having no reservations or doubts; unquestioning or unconditional; usually said of faith or trust.
ex: He is not only a zealous advocate for pusilanimous and passive obedience, but for the most implicit faith in the dictatorial mandates of power.

s.def: entangled, twisted together.
ex: In his deep fleece […] I cling implicit.

s.def: Suggested without being stated directly; implicated or hinted at.
ex: her implied disapproval of the plan

s.def: simple past and past participle of imply

ety: Back-formation from implosion.

s.def: To collapse or burst inward violently.
ex: The submarine imploded as it sank below its crush depth.

s.def: To cause to collapse or burst inward violently.
The opposite of explode, array to string conversion.
To compress (data) with a particular algorithm.

ety: PIE word *h₁én The verb is borrowed from Middle French implorer (modern French implorer (“to beg, plead, implore”)), or directly from its etymon Latin implōrāre, the present active infinitive of implōrō (“to beseech, entreat, implore; to appeal to, pray to”), from im- (a variant of in- (intensifying prefix)) + plōrō (“to cry out; to complain, deplore, lament”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₃(w)- (“to flow; to swim”)). The noun is derived from the verb.

s.def: To beg or plead for (something) earnestly or urgently; to beseech.
ex: My daily bread is litt'rally implor'd, / I have no barns nor granaries to hoard; […]

s.def: To beg or plead that (someone) earnestly or urgently do something; to beseech, to entreat.
ex: Talk not thus, I implore you, Evelyn: do not imagine me the worldly calculator that my enemies deem me.
A prayer lies bound in me / And implores a god, / And implores a name.

s.def: Often followed by for (a thing) or of (a person): to express an earnest or urgent plea.
ex: That fortnight Rochester passed in intriguing and imploring.
"Do not let me think of them too often, too much, too fondly," I implored; […]

s.def: An act of begging or pleading earnestly or urgently; an entreaty, an imploration or imploring, a plea.

ety: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.

s.def: To have as a necessary consequence; to lead to (something) as a consequence.
ex: Correlation does not imply causation
The proposition that "all dogs are mammals" implies that my dog is a mammal.

s.def: To suggest by logical inference.
ex: When I state that your dog is brown, I am not implying that all dogs are brown.

s.def: To hint; to insinuate; to suggest tacitly and avoid a direct statement.
ex: What do you mean "we need to be more careful with hygiene"? Are you implying that I don't wash my hands?
Naturally, the river wasn't wrinkled or creased at all— wrong words, implying something unfluid like skin, something unenduring, prey to age.

s.def: To enfold, entangle.
ex: And in his bosome secretly there lay / An hatefull Snake, the which his taile vptyes / In many folds, and mortall sting implyes.

s.def: The state or act of being impolitic.
ex: An impulse urged him to plant a sudden blow on it, by he forced himself to consider the impolicy of such an act.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin impolītus. Equivalent to im- + polite.

s.def: Not polite; discourteous; not of polished manners; wanting in good manners.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English im- English politic English impolitic From im- + politic.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. s.def: Not ponderable; without sensible or appreciable weight; incapable of being weighed.
Difficult or impossible to comprehend or evaluate.

A substance or body, which is not ponderable, i.e., which not does not having a detectable amount of matter or measurable mass. An imponderable substance or body; specifically, in the plural, a name formerly applied to heat, light, electricity, and magnetism.
An imponderable question.
A factor that cannot be anticipated.

ety: From Middle English importen, from Old French emporter, importer, from Latin importō (“bring in from abroad, import”, verb), from in (“in, at, on; into”) + portō (“to carry, bear; convey”).

s.def: Something brought in from an exterior source, especially for sale or trade.
The practice of importing.
A foreigner playing in a sports league.
To bring (something) in from a foreign country, especially for sale or trade.
ex: Nauru imports foods from Australia because phosphate mining destroyed land for farming.

s.def: To load a file into a software application from another version or system.
ex: How can I import files from older versions of this application?

s.def: To be important; to be significant; to be of consequence.
ex: See how much it importeth to learn to take Time by the Fore-Top.

s.def: To be of importance to (someone or something).
ex: This Letter is mistooke: it importeth none here: It is writ to laquenetta.
If I endure it, what imports it you?

s.def: To be incumbent on (someone to do something).
ex: It imports us to get all the aid and assistance we can.

s.def: To be important or crucial to (that something happen).
ex: It much imports your house That all should be made clear.

s.def: To mean, signify.

ety: From Middle English importaunce, from Middle French importance, from Medieval Latin importantia. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ance.

s.def: The quality or condition of being important or worthy of note.
ex: The recording speed is also of importance in detecting flutters of high frequency.

s.def: significance or prominence.
personal status or standing.
Something of importance.

ety: From Middle English important, from Medieval Latin important-, importāns. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ant. Displaced native Old English hēah and hefiġ.

s.def: Having relevant and crucial value; having import.
ex: We thought it important for there to be a fire escape at the back of every building.

s.def: Pompous; self-important.

ety: Etymology tree English import Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English importer From import + -er.

ex: India is the world's biggest importer of gold.

ety: First attested in 1477, in Middle english; from Latin importūnus + -ate (adjective-forming suffix), modelled on Middle French importuné. By surface analysis, importune + -ate (compare inopportune). The noun was substantivized from the adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

s.def: Persistent or pressing, often annoyingly so.
ex: Trembling in every limb I raise my loud im­portunate cry, And in a sacred terror wait the Delian god’s reply.

s.def: Given to importunate demands, greedily or thoughtlessly demanding.
ex: [...] if you reprimand or punish them, be assured every one will consider you importunate as well as ridiculous.

s.def: An importuner.
ex: This will put an Answer into the Kings mouth, against all importunates.

s.def: To importune, or to obtain by importunity.
ex: Is my work ended? The fear of importunating my friends answers, “Yes.”
It is the concrete that impresses, that importunates until it influences—in writing as in everything else.

ety: From Middle French importuner and its etymon Medieval Latin importūnor (“to make oneself troublesome”), from Latin importūnus (“unfit, troublesome”), originally "having no harbor".

s.def: To harass with persistent requests.
To bother, irritate, trouble.
ex: But I will no longer importune my young cousin.

s.def: To approach to offer one's services as a prostitute, or otherwise make improper proposals.
To import; to signify.
ex: It importunes death.

s.def: Grievous, severe, exacting.
ex: And therewithall he fiercely at him flew, / And with importune outrage him assayld [...].

s.def: Inopportune; unseasonable.
Troublesome; vexatious; persistent.
ex: And their importune fates all satisfide.

s.def: Synonym of importuner.

ety: From Late Middle English importunitie, importunyte (“insistence, persistence; grievance; hardship, trouble; inappropriateness (?)”), from Anglo-Norman importunité, and Middle French importunité (“persistent demand; hardship, trouble; something difficult or troublesome; inappropriateness”) (modern French importunité), and their etymon Latin importūnitās (“insolence, rudeness; oppressiveness, relentlessness; unfitness, unsuitableness”), from importūnus (“annoying; rude; inconvenient; unsuitable”)…

s.def: Constant and insistent demanding or proposing, especially if regarded as annoying or upsetting; also, the character of such behaviour; (countable) an instance of this.

s.def: The fact of being at an inappropriate or unsuitable time; unseasonableness.

ex: [S]uch vague memories hang about the mind like cobwebs, with tickling importunity—best to sweep them away at a dash: […]

s.def: The quality of being annoying or troublesome; difficulty, trouble; (countable) an instance of this.

ety: The verb is derived from Late Middle English imposen (“to place, set; to impose (a duty, etc.)”), borrowed from Middle French imposer, and Old French emposer, enposer (“to impose (a duty, tax, etc.)”) (modern French imposer), from im-, em- (variants of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + poser (“to place, put”), modelled after: * Latin impōnere (“to place or set (something) on; (figurative) to impose (a duty, tax, etc.)”), from im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘on, upon’)) + pōnō (“to place,…

s.def: To physically lay or place (something) on another thing; to deposit, to put, to set.

ex: Congress imposed new tariffs.

New Jersey was reeling on Wednesday from the impact of Hurricane Sandy, […] Localities across New Jersey imposed curfews to prevent looting.

s.def: To place or put (something chiefly immaterial, especially something regarded as burdensome as a duty, an encumbrance, a penalty, etc.) on another thing or on someone; to inflict, to repose; also, to place or put (on someone a chiefly immaterial thing, especially something regarded as burdensome).

Master should measure strength with master, then, / Before the servant be imposed a task.

s.def: To force or put (a thing) on someone or something by deceit or stealth; to foist, to obtrude.

To accuse someone of (a crime, or a sin or other wrongdoing); to charge, to impute.
To put (a conclusion or end) to something definitively.
Chiefly followed by on or upon.

s.def: An act of placing or putting on something chiefly immaterial, especially something regarded as burdensome as a duty, a task, etc.; an imposition.

An unwelcome burden, presence, or obligation.
ex: He expunges his own anguish at his diagnosis with HIV and the impositions that have claimed his freedom.

s.def: That which is imposed, levied, or enjoined.
A trick or deception put or laid on others.
Arrangement of a printed product’s pages on the printer's sheet so as to have the pages in proper order in the final product.
A practice of laying hands on a person in a religious ceremony; used e.g. in confirmation and ordination.
A task imposed on a student as punishment.

ex: 13 March 1962, John F. Kennedy, speech at the White House Those who make peaceful revolution impossible will make violent revolution inevitable.

ex: You never listen to a word I say – you're impossible!
This humidity is impossible.
I never met a more impossible girl.

s.def: imaginary
ex: impossible quantities, or imaginary numbers

“Ye can't expect impossibles, and Jim hadn't no idee o' takin' yer trunk along of him in ther buggy when he kem hyar this mornin'.
For one thing, the Gospel's moral impossibles appear, in this light, not as an objection to Christianity, but as one of its most striking evidences.

s.def: A skateboard trick consisting of a backflip performed in midair.

ex: Technology without morality is barbarous; morality without technology is impotent

ex: A person smeared with the excrement of a mouse was rendered impotent, according to Pliny the Elder.

Lacking self-restraint
A man who has erectile dysfunction
An impotent or powerless person

ex: His car was impounded after he parked it illegally.

to impound a document for safekeeping.

ex: I already checked that out, and Keller has never called to get it out of impound.

s.def: Amounts collected from a debtor and held by one with a security interest in property for payment of property taxes and insurance.

ety: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

To become poor.
To weaken in quality; to deprive of some strength or richness.
ex: That exuberant crop quickly impoverishes any fertile soil.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English im- English practicable English impracticable From im- + practicable.

impassable (of a passage or road)
unmanageable

s.def: Not practical; impracticable.

ety: Borrowed from Latin imprecātus, perfect active participle of imprecor (“to invoke (good or evil) upon, pray to, call upon”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“upon”) + precor (“to pray”).

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English im- English precise English imprecise From im- + precise.

ex: Rushdie oxymoronically notes that Hobson-Jobson ‘can be wonderfully imprecise at times’ (1985: 82).

ety: From Late Middle English imprenable, impregnable (“impossible to capture, impregnable”), from Old French imprenable (modern French imprenable (“impregnable”)), from im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + prenable (“(military) of a building, position, etc.: takable”) (from prendre (“to take”) + -able (suffix meaning ‘creating an effect or influence’)). ex: Jurgis got up, wild with rage; but the door was shut and the great castle was dark and impregnable.

s.def: Too strong to be defeated or overcome; invincible.
Capable of being impregnated; impregnatable.
ex: The reproductive strategies of troop members, especially those of impregnable females, are suggested to influence patterns of range use.

ety: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). ex: To Tartarize, ta²r'ta⁴r-i¹ze, v. a. To impregnate with tartar.

To fertilize.
To become pregnant.

s.def: Impregnated (all senses).
Pregnant, with child.
Rendered fruitful, prolific.
Imbued, saturated, permeated or filled with.
Impregnable.

s.def: A manager or producer in the entertainment industry, especially music or theatre.

ety: From Middle French imprescriptible, corresponding to im- + prescriptible.

ex: Freedom is, indeed, the natural and imprescriptible right of man […].

Proto-Italic *pres- Latin premō Latin imprimō Latin impressusder. Middle English impressen English impress From Middle English impressen, from Latin impressus, perfect passive participle of imprimere (“to press into or upon, stick, stamp, or dig into”), from in (“in, upon”) + premere (“to press”).

ex: You impressed me with your command of Urdu.
Okay, so you're a rocket scientist / That don't impress me much

ex: We impressed our footprints in the wet cement.
Then he impresses the die into the clay to produce a design on the surface.

ex: The money was impressed into the hands of the financial ministry.

ex: The press gang used to impress people into the Navy.

ex: Some prefer a double action gun because it seems more foolproof in the heat of the moment when someone might not be thinking calmly.

w: in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king
ety: Calque of Latin in regione caecorum rex est luscus, popularized by Desiderius Erasmus’ Adagia (1500). For further origin compare Aramaic בשוק סמייא צווחין לעווירא סגי נהור (literally “in the street of the blind, the one-eyed man is called the guiding light”), found in the Genesis Rabbah (4th or 5th century CE). This may be Erasmus’ direct source, but at least some traditional link between both forms seems likely.

s.def: Even someone with limited abilities or opportunities is dominant over, and considered special by, those who have even fewer abilities and opportunities; the value of any ability depends on its prevalence.
tr: körler ülkesinde tek gözü olan kral olur

s.def: Disposed (to do something or for something; often romantic or sexual, without further context).
ex: Don’t start with me: I’m not in the mood.
He wasn't in the mood to tango.
I'm in the mood for love, simply because you're near me.

s.def: Within a short period of time.
At the last possible moment; at the last minute.
ex: He finished writing his paper and slid it under the door just in the nick of time.
In the nick of time he lassoed with a trounce / the low-down villains who had stubbed our toes.
Sir Frances stopped midrant, and just in the nick of time, for his next words would have been "veriest whipster,"

s.def: In trouble.
ex: [U]nless the murderer came back, I had till about six o'clock in the morning for my cogitations. I was in the soup — that was pretty clear.
[T]he poor old lad is absolutely dependent on that remittance of yours, and when you cut it off, don't you know, he was pretty solidly in the soup.

s.def: In relation to; in connection with; with respect to.
ex: He had seen Death many times, - met him in the way of trade, and got acquainted with him.
Of what that involves in the way of doctrine I have no idea nor the time to inform myself.
Certainly their extracurricular talents in the way of sport have not gone unnoticed.

s.def: In or into a position of being likely to obtain, to attain, or to achieve.
ex: The King sought out the farmer who had been branded and sold as a slave . . . and put him in the way of a comfortable livelihood.
But it would certainly put her in the way of a grand marriage.

s.def: Similar to; as an instance of; as a kind of.
ex: I don't think there's anything in the way of a haircut or a shave or a shampoo that could make me like my girl any less.

s.def: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see in the way, of.
Living and roaming freely in nature; not domesticated.
ex: But during its lifetime, a single macaw left in the wild might yield more than 16 times as much in tourist income.

s.def: At large.
ex: A new, deadly type of virus has been detected in the wild.

s.def: In practical use, as opposed to in a dictionary or wordlist.
ex: This word is very rare; it may be difficult to find usages of it in the wild.

s.def: By coincidence in the course of everyday life.
ex: I'd seen this stock photo in memes a hundred times, but yesterday I saw it in the wild, illustrating a magazine article.

s.def: At or before the time assigned.
ex: I would have died had I not been gottten to hospital in time.

s.def: As time passes.
ex: In time, it got easier to deal with her death.
He'll understand in time that you were trying to help him.

s.def: Sufficiently early.
ex: You've got here in time for tea — I was just making some.

s.def: In rhythm.
ex: Am I in time with/to the music?

s.def: At the same rhythm as.
In the correct tempo.

s.def: Without success or a result; ending in failure.

s.def: In a disrespectful manner, without honoring the proper meaning; insincerely or without proper respect.

s.def: The fertilization of an ovum by sperm outside of a woman's body; normally used as a treatment for infertility.

Incarnato is derived from Ecclesiastical Latin and Late Latin incarnātus (“having been made incarnate”), the perfect passive participle of incarnō (“to become or make incarnate; to make into flesh”), from in- (suffix meaning ‘in, ins…

s.def: Of the pale pink or pale red colour of flesh; carnation.
Of the blood-red colour of raw flesh; crimson.
ex: The bandages on his hands – cerise and incarnadine, opalescent and viridian – were grotesqueries that only emphasised his stature.

s.def: Bloodstained, bloody.
Of a red colour.
ex: Let the wine incarnadine, / In crystal goblets gleaming, / Be the sign, O muse divine, / Of golden moments teeming.
Green orchards with ripe fruit incarnadine, / Each several member autumn-canopied / So thickly as to bend beneath its freight, [...]

s.def: The pale pink or pale red colour of flesh; carnation.
The blood-red colour of raw flesh; crimson.
A red colour.
ex: Now sixty-eight years of age she [Elizabeth I] has chosen for the occasion of a dance in her honor a long flowing velvet gown of incarnadine red.

s.def: To make flesh-coloured.
To make red, especially blood-coloured or crimson; to redden.
ex: And he, who turn'd the waters into blood, / Shall next incarnadine these desart sands, / Whilst dogs and vultures hunt us on the track.
When I repeat to Moody my father's tribute such a sudden wine-dark flush incarnadines his face that I am startled.
"And what of all the men you shot in Malaya and the Indies?" he asked. "What did you think when their blood incarnadined the oceans of Asia? Tell me!"

ety: First attested in 1395, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English incarnat(e) (“(of God or Christ) embodied in human form or flesh, incarnate; provided with new tissues, healed; (with devel, in curses) bloody”), borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, perfect passive participle of incarnor (“to be made flesh, become incarnate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- + Latin carō (“flesh”, carn- in its oblique stem) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + La…

s.def: Embodied in flesh; given a bodily, especially a human, form; personified.
Flesh-colored; crimson.
ex: Yards of Turkey silk incarnate.

s.def: To embody in flesh; to invest with a bodily, especially a human, form.
ex: For one thing, we virtually decided that these morbidities and the hellish Himalayan Mi-Go were one and the same order of incarnated nightmare.
Not all of the soul can incarnate into a body; the part which is left above is the psyche.

s.def: To gain full existence (bodily or otherwise).
ex: SCP-3125 incarnated the following winter.

s.def: To incarn; to become covered with flesh; to heal over.
To make carnal; to reduce the spiritual nature of.
ex: This essence to incarnate and imbrute, / That to the height of deity aspired.

s.def: To put into or represent in a concrete form, as an idea.
Not in the flesh; spiritual.
ex: I fear nothing […] that devil carnate or incarnate can fairly do.

ety: From Middle English incarnacion, borrowed from Old French incarnacion, from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin incarnatio, from Late Latin incarnari (“to be made flesh”).

s.def: An incarnate being or form.
ex: She is a new incarnation of some of the illustrious dead.
Robespierre, the very incarnation of lustful and deadly Vengeance, stands silently by..

s.def: A version or iteration (of something).
A living being embodying a deity or spirit.
An assumption of human form or nature.
A person or thing regarded as embodying or exhibiting some quality, idea, or the like.
ex: The leading dancer is the incarnation of grace.

s.def: The act of incarnating.
The state of being incarnated.
A rosy or red colour; flesh (the colour); carnation.
The process of healing wounds and filling the part with new flesh; granulation.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English case English incase From in- + case.

s.def: Alternative spelling of encase.
Misspelling of in case.

ety: From incase + -ment.

s.def: Archaic form of encasement.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English cautious English incautious From in- (negative prefix) + cautious.

s.def: careless, reckless, not exercising proper caution.
ex: "You might have remained so still," replies Jones, "if you had not been unfortunate, I will venture to say incautious, in the placing your affections.
Pot-plants on spindle-legged stands lurked in wait for an incautious gesture.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- Middle English voluntarie English voluntary English involuntarysyl. abbr. Latin caelebslbor. English -ate English celibatesyl. abbr. English incel Syllabic abbreviation of involuntary celibate. Coined by "Alana" in 1997 on an online forum (originally as invcel). Came to widespread usage in the mid-2010s, chiefly online, but now more widespread.

s.def: Someone (especially a man) who desires a sexual relationship but considers themselves unable to attract a partner; (often specifically), a member of an online subculture of people who identify in this way, often adopting resentful or misogynistic attitudes towards women as a result.
ex: Though, involuntary celibates (or incels) shouldn't try to rationalize a dateless season or pass off sexual awkwardness as virtue; […]
The incel ideology has already inspired the murders of at least sixteen people.
Who are the ‘incels’ and how do they relate to Toronto van attack?

s.def: "Involuntary celibacy": the state of being not sexually active despite wishing to be.

ety: From Middle English incendiarie, from Old French incendiaire, from Latin incendiārius (“setting alight”), from incendium (“destructive fire”), from incendō (“to set on fire, kindle”), from in- (“into, in, on, upon”) + candeō (“to be hot”).

s.def: Capable of, or used for, or actually causing fire.
Of a damaging fire, intentionally caused rather than accidental.
Intentionally stirring up strife, riot, rebellion.
Inflammatory, emotionally charged.
ex: Politics is an incendiary topic; it tends to cause fights to break out.

s.def: Something capable of causing fire, particularly a weapon.
ex: The military used incendiaries to destroy the building. Fortunately, the fire didn't spread.

s.def: One who maliciously sets fires.
One who excites or inflames factions into quarrels.
ex: March 7, 1692, Richard Bentley, The Folly of Atheism Several cities […] drove them out as incendiaries.

ety: From Middle English encens, from Old French encens (“sweet-smelling substance”) from Late Latin incensum (“burnt incense”, literally “something burnt”), neuter past participle of incendō (“to set on fire”). Compare incendiary. Doublet of incienso. Displaced native Old English rēcels.

s.def: material burnt for fragrant smoke
Biotic material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, often used in religious rites or for aesthetic reasons.
The fragrant smoke released by burning incense (sense 1).
Homage; adulation.
To set on fire; to inflame; to kindle; to burn.
To anger; to infuriate.
ex: I think it would incense him to learn the truth.

s.def: To offer incense to.
To perfume with, or as with, incense.
ex: Neither, for the future, shall any man or woman, self-styled noble, be incensed,—foolishly fumigated with incense, in Church; as the wont has been.
The priests solemnly incensed the girl who personated the goddess.

s.def: To incite; to stimulate.

ety: From Medieval Latin incentīvus (“that strikes up or sets the tune”), from incinō (“to strike up”), from in- (“in, on”) + canō (“to sing”) + -ive. The formation appears to have been influenced by incendō (“to set on fire”).

s.def: Something that motivates, rouses, or encourages.
ex: I have no incentive to do housework right now.

s.def: A bonus or reward, often monetary, to work harder.
ex: Management offered the sales team a $500 incentive for each car sold.

s.def: Inciting; encouraging or moving; rousing to action; stimulating.
ex: Competency is of all other proportions the most incentive to industry.

s.def: Serving to kindle or set on fire.
ex: Part incentive reed / Provide, pernicious with one touch of fire.

ety: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin inceptiō, from inceptus, perfect passive participle of incipiō (“to begin”). The layering sense derives from the 2010 science fiction film Inception, in which a team of people infiltrate someone’s subconscious mind, proceeding through several layers of dreams with the goal of causing the target to incept an idea.

s.def: The creation or beginning of something; the establishment.
ex: From its inception, the agency has been helping people obtain and properly install car seats for children.
My mother, at my inception, did not create that passionate lack of fear that is mine.

s.def: A layering, nesting, or recursion of something within itself.
ex: Well it's the… Mr. Introspective / I'm a dreamer's dream, a sort of an inception
I look at you, I see my reflection / Three levels deep, this is inception
He was sketching me as I doodled in my own book, almost like an inception.

ety: From Middle French incertitude.

s.def: uncertainty, doubt, insecurity

ety: From Late Middle English incessaunte, from Late Latin incessāns, incessantem, from Latin in- + cessāns.

s.def: Without pause or stop; not ending, especially to the point of annoyance.
ex: The dog's incessant barking kept the girl awake all night.
[…] incessant interferings and bickerings, in every country, between the secular powers and the ecclesiastical.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin incestus. Displaced Old English mǣġhǣmed (literally “relative-sex”). Doublet of inchaste.

s.def: Sexual relations between close relatives, especially immediate family members and sometimes first cousins, usually considered taboo.
ex: Genetic problems caused by incest are thought to have plagued many royal families in the Middle Ages.
He was only Craster's whelp, an abomination born of incest, not the son of the King-beyond-the-Wall.

s.def: Romantic relationships between close relatives, also widely taboo.
To engage in incestuous sexual activities.
ex: I do not want anyone to feel that my lesbianism is a result of being incested.
Her erotic transference ultimately devolved into a revelation that she had been consistently incested by her brother

ety: Etymology tree English incest Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Old French -usbor. Middle English -ous English -ous English incestuous From incest + -ous.

s.def: Pertaining to or engaging in incest.
ex: If you engaged in an incestuous relationship with a family member, that would make you an inbreeder.

s.def: Characterized by mutual relationships that are intimate and exclusive to the detriment of outsiders.
ex: Democrats have the luxury of controlling the public narrative, thanks, in large part, to their incestuous relationship with the news media.

ety: From Middle English ynche, enche, from Old English ynċe, borrowed from Latin ū̆ncia (“Roman inch, various similar units”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). Doublet of ounce, uncia, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

s.def: An English unit of length equal to 1/12 of a foot or 2.54 cm.
ex: One rule of thumb is that the width of an adult thumb can approximate a length of one inch.
The term "precision measurement" […] refers to the art of reproducing and controlling dimensions expressed in thousandths of an inch or smaller.

s.def: Any very short distance.
ex: Don't move an inch!
Beldame, I think we watched you at an inch.
[B]e the consequences what they may, they shall not move an inch, nor a hair's-breadth from the ground of their groundless spiritual independence, […]

s.def: Any of various similar units of length in other traditional systems of measurement.
ex: At the time of Augustus, the Roman inch was standardized at a length about 3% shorter than the modern English one.

s.def: A depth of one inch on the ground, used as a measurement of rainfall.
ex: Expect around 2 inches of rain on Saturday afternoon.

s.def: A depth of one inch in a glass, used as a rough measurement of alcoholic beverages.
ex: My partner only drinks about a 1 inch pour with dinner, leaving the rest of the bottle for me.

s.def: To advance very slowly, or by a small amount (in a particular direction).
ex: Fearful of falling, he inched along the window ledge.
On reaching the section under construction they must be capable of inching the train forward on rough track up gradients as steep as 1 in 30.

s.def: To drive by inches, or small degrees.
ex: He gets too far into the soldier's grace / And inches out my master.

s.def: To deal out by inches; to give sparingly.
A small island; an islet.
ex: The blackening wave is edged with white; / To inch and rock the sea-mews fly.

s.def: A meadow, pasture, field, or haugh.

der: a mile wide and an inch deep

ety: From inch + -meal.

s.def: Gradually, little by little (an inch at a time).
ex: All the infections that the sun sucks up / From bogs, fens, flats, on Prosper fall, and make him / By inch-meal a disease!
Those who are not thus slippery in the tail, are light of finger; and of these the most pernicious are those who beggar you inchmeal.
I am a sanguinary murderer of time, and would kill him inchmeal just now.

ety: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb circa 1631; borrowed from Latin incohātus (“begun, unfinished”), perfect passive participle of incohō (“to begin”), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Cognate with Spanish incoar (“to initiate, commence, begin”).

s.def: Recently started but not fully formed yet; just begun; only elementary or immature.
ex: neither a substance perfect, nor a substance inchoate
...unfortunately, we have to face inchoate schemes which will demand the utmost jealousy and vigilance of Parliament.
The private conception of any breach of law is apt to be inspiriting, for the scheme (while yet inchoate) wears dashing and attractive colours.

s.def: Chaotic, disordered, confused; also, incoherent, rambling.
Of a crime, imposing criminal liability for an incompleted act.
A beginning, an immature start.
To begin or start (something).
To cause or bring about. In the field of criminology, to encourage, assist, conspire, aid and abet, incite, etc.
To make a start.

ety: From inch + worm. So called because their gradual movement seems to be measuring the ground; compare measuring worm.

s.def: The larva of a moth of the family Geometridae.
To move in a looping fashion, like an inchworm.
To crawl or creep slowly.

ety: From Middle French incidence, from Medieval Latin incidentia (“a falling upon”), from Latin incidens, present participle of incidere (“to fall upon”), from in (“on”) + cadere (“to fall”).

s.def: The act of something happening; occurrence.
The extent or the relative frequency of something happening.
The manner of falling; bearing or onus, as of a tax that falls unequally.
The striking of radiation or a projectile upon a surface.
A measure of the rate of new occurrence of a given medical condition in a population within a specified period of time.
The falling of a point on a line, or a line on a plane.
The relation between an edge of a graph and one of the vertices it connects.

ety: Recorded since 1412, from Middle French incident, from Latin incidens, the present active participle of incidō (“to happen, befall”), itself from in- (“on”) + -cidō, the combining form of cadō (“to fall”).

s.def: An event or occurrence.
ex: She could not recall the time of the incident.
It was an incident that he hoped to forget.
The suspect was released without further incident.

s.def: event causing interruption or crisis
A (relatively minor) event that is incidental to, or related to others.
An event that causes or may cause an interruption or a crisis, such as a workplace illness or a software error.
Arising as the result of an event, inherent.
ex: No major hazards incident to this job.

s.def: Falling on or striking a surface.
ex: The incident light illuminated the surface.

s.def: Coming or happening accidentally; not in the usual course of things; not in connection with the main design; not according to expectation; casual; fortuitous.
Liable to happen; apt to occur; befalling; hence, naturally happening or appertaining.
ex: All chances incident to mans frail life.
17th century, Richard Milward, "Preface" to Seldeniana the studies incident to his profession

s.def: Dependent upon, or appertaining to, another thing, called the principal.
In a relation of incidence
ex: The second inequality follows from the fact that all the edges incident with a fixed vertex separate [an arbitrary graph] G.

ety: From incident + -al.

s.def: Loosely associated; of limited relevance except indirectly; only accidentally related.
ex: That character, though colorful, is incidental to the overall plot.
incidental evidence

s.def: Occurring by chance.
Existing tangentially, being a byproduct, a tangent, or a likely consequence.
ex: Injuries are incidental to contact sports: they're going to happen.

s.def: Entering or approaching, prior to reflection (more frequently incident).
Minor items, not further defined. Incidental expense.
ex: She's costing us a lot in incidentals.

s.def: Something that is incidental.

ety: Etymology tree English incidental Middle English -ly English -ly English incidentally From incidental + -ly.

s.def: In an incidental manner.
ex: Near-synonyms: coincidentally, happenstantially, circumstantially, by chance, accidentally, semirandomly, randomly

ety: From Latin incinerātus, perfect participle of incinerō (“to burn into ashes”), from cinis (“ashes”).

s.def: To destroy by burning.
ex: His mother was incinerated in the Dresden fire-storm. So it goes.

s.def: To annihilate (not necessarily by burning).

ety: Borrowed from Latin incipiēns, present participle of incipiō (“begin”).

s.def: In an initial stage; beginning, starting, coming into existence.
ex: After 500 years, incipient towns appeared.
Employees shall be familiarized with the use of a fire extinguisher in incipient stage fire fighting.
It need not be supposed that all varieties or incipient species necessarily attain the rank of species.

s.def: A beginner.
A verb tense of the Hebrew language.

ety: From Middle French inciser.

s.def: To cut in or into with a sharp instrument; to carve; to engrave.
ex: The executioner’s blade is incised with Christ’s crown of thorns, and with the words of a prayer.

ety: From Middle English inscicioun, from Middle French incision, from Late Latin incisiō from the verb incidō (“to cut into”) + action noun suffix -iō.

s.def: A cut, especially one made by a scalpel or similar medical tool in the context of surgical operation; the scar resulting from such a cut.
ex: Gunch was so humorous that Mrs. Babbitt said he must “stop making her laugh because honestly it was hurting her incision.”

s.def: The act of cutting into a substance.
ex: Mnesarchus, early as a sculptor known, From nice incision of the costly stone,
Slowly, as meticulously as if engaged upon a surgical incision, Mr Nox opened his mail.

s.def: Separation or solution of viscid matter by medicines.
A cut-back
ex: Riyad Mahrez also dragged wide after a De Bruyne incision.

ety: Late Middle English (in the sense “cutting, penetrating”), borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus, from incīdō (“to cut in, cut through”) + -īvus (“-ive”, adjectival suffix). Compare Middle French incisif.

s.def: Intelligently analytical and concise. (of a person or mental process)
Quickly proceeding to judgment and forceful in expression. (of an action)
ex: An incisive producer, who expressed vehement disapproval with my pitch upon my first sentence.

s.def: Having the quality of incising, cutting, or penetrating, as with a sharp instrument; trenchant.
ex: An incisive, high voice.
And her incisive smile accrediting / That treason of false witness in my blush.

s.def: Of or relating to the incisors.
ex: the incisive bones, the premaxillaries

s.def: A narrow-edged tooth at the front of the mouth of mammals, between the canines and adapted for cutting; in humans there are four in each jaw.

ety: From Middle French inciter, from Latin incitō (“to set in motion, hasten, urge, incite”), from in (“in, on”) + citō (“to set in motion, urge”), frequentative of cieō (“to rouse, excite, call”).

s.def: To instigate a specific incident.
To call into action.
ex: The judge was told by the accused that his friends had incited him to commit the crime.
incite people to violence
Human rights groups blame the anti-Rohingya propaganda for inciting murders, rapes and the largest forced human migration in recent history.

s.def: To entreat an act.

ety: From Middle French incivilité, from Late Latin incivilitas (“incivility”), from Latin incivilis (“impolite, uncivil”), from in- (privative prefix) + civilis (“belonging to a citizen, civic, political, urbane, courteous, civil”) (from civis (“a citizen”)), equivalent to in- + civility.

s.def: The state of being uncivil; lack of courtesy; rudeness in manner.
ex: Courtezan. How say you now? is not your husband mad? / Adriana. His incivility confirms no less.
[S]he could not bear incivility to her guests, to young men in particular, […]

s.def: Any act of rudeness or ill-breeding.
Lack of civilization; a state of rudeness or barbarism.

ety: From Latin inclēmēns (“unmerciful, severe”), from in- (“not”) + clēmēns (“mild, placid”).

s.def: Stormy, of rough weather; not clement.
ex: inclement weather

s.def: Merciless, unrelenting.
Unmercifully severe in temper or action.

ety: From incline + -able.

s.def: Capable of being inclined or tilted.
ex: an inclinable desk

s.def: Capable of being inclined, or given a tendency.
ex: He seemed inclinable to peace, if we negotiated skilfully.

ety: From Middle English inclinacioun, inclinacyon, from Old French inclination and Latin inclīnātiō. Morphologically incline + -ation.

s.def: A physical tilt or bend.
ex: The inclination of his head increased and he awoke with a start.

s.def: A slant or slope.
ex: The road up to the house had a steep inclination.

s.def: A tendency.
ex: His inclination to drink escalated to alcoholism.

s.def: The angle of intersection of a reference plane.
ex: The astronomer calculated the inclination of the equator or ecliptic of Earth and the orbital planes of each visible heavenly body.
Artillery must take account of a weapon's precise inclination.

s.def: A person or thing loved or admired.
ex: c. 1672-1679, William Temple, Memoirs you make will be a Discovery of your Inclinations

s.def: To bend or move (something) out of a given plane or direction, often the horizontal or vertical.
ex: He had to incline his body against the gusts to avoid being blown down in the storm.
The people following the coffin inclined their heads in grief.

s.def: To slope.
ex: Over the centuries the wind made the walls of the farmhouse incline.

s.def: To tend to do or believe something, or move or be moved in a certain direction, away from a point of view, attitude, etc.
ex: He inclines to believe anything he reads in the newspapers.
I'm inclined to give up smoking after hearing of the risks to my health.

s.def: A slope.
ex: To reach the building, we had to climb a steep incline.
The incline can be altered to any grade so as to suit the weight of the door or gate to which the butt is attached.

s.def: A portal of a subway tunnel.
ex: the Pleasant Street Incline

ety: Etymology tree Latin inclīnāre Old French enclinerbor. Middle English enclinen English incline Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. English -o- English -meter English inclinometer From incline + -o- + -meter.

s.def: An instrument that displays the angle of an aircraft relative to the horizon.
An instrument that measures magnetic dip; a dip circle.
A surveying instrument that measures angles of inclination or elevation; a clinometer.
Archaic spelling of enclose.
ex: From the stock, as well as from the branches, rises a jonquil flower, the pistil of which contains the husk which incloses the fruit.

ety: From Middle English includen, borrowed from Latin inclūdere (“to shut in, enclose, insert”), from in- (“in”) + claudere (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“key, hook, nail”). Doublet of enclose. Displaced native Old English belūcan (“to include,” also “to shut in”).

s.def: To bring into a group, class, set, or total as a (new) part or member.
ex: I will purchase the vacation package if you will include car rental.

s.def: To enclose, confine.
ex: I could have here willingly ranged, but these straits wherein I am included will not permit.

s.def: To consider as part of something; to comprehend.
ex: The vacation package includes car rental.
Does this volume of Shakespeare include his sonnets?
I was included in the invitation to the family gathering.

s.def: To conclude; to terminate.
ex: Come, let us go; we will include all jars / With triumphs, mirth, and rare solemnity.

s.def: To use a directive that allows the use of source code from another file.
ex: You have to include the strings library to use this function.

s.def: A piece of source code or other content that is dynamically retrieved for inclusion in another item.
ex: In the previous lesson, you learned how to use server-side includes, which enable you to easily include snippets of web pages within other web pages.

ety: By surface analysis, include + -ing.

s.def: Such as, among which; introducing one or more parts of the group or topic just mentioned.
ex: All this has led to an explosion of protest across China, including among a middle class that has discovered nimbyism.
All you have to do is to fill in the details, including your name and address and the amount you wish to give.

s.def: Introducing a finite clause.

s.def: An addition or annex to a group, set, or total.
ex: The poem was a new inclusion in the textbook.

s.def: The act of including, i.e. adding or annexing, (something) to a group, set, or total.
ex: The inclusion of the poem added value to the course.

s.def: Anything foreign that is included in a material.
Any material that is trapped inside a mineral during its formation, as a defect in a precious stone.
ex: The fewer inclusions a diamond has, the better is its clarity and value. Often the inclusions can be cut out of a diamond in the rough.

s.def: A nuclear or cytoplasmic aggregate of stainable substances.
An object completely inside a tissue, such as epidermal inclusion cyst, a cyst in the epidermis.
A mapping where the domain is a subset of the image.
Restriction; limitation.

An incommensurable value or quantity; an irrational number.

ety: From in- + communicative.

ety: From Middle English incorrigible, from Middle French incorrigible (1334), or directly from Latin incorrigibilis (“not to be corrected”), from in- (“not”) + corrigere (“to correct”) + -ibilis (“-able”), equivalent to in- + corrigible. Recorded since 1340.

ex: The statement "My knee hurts" is incorrigible.

s.def: Impossible to cure.

s.def: An incorrigibly bad person.

ex: The Moon increases.

s.def: For a quantity, the act or process of becoming larger.

ex: An increase of about 30% in hits on the website.

Any situation in which the outcome cannot be completely predicted in advance.

The index finger; the forefinger.

A number representing a property or ratio; a coefficient.
A raised suffix indicating a power.

ety: Borrowed from Latin indicātus, perfect passive participle of indicō (“to point out, indicate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, to”) + dicō (“to declare, (originally) to point”). See also diction and index.

ety: From Old French indication, from Latin indicātiō (“a showing, indicating the value of something; valuation”), from indicō (“point out, indicate, show; value”); see indicate; compare French indication, Spanish indicación, Italian indicazione. By surface analysis, indicate + -ion.

A discovery made; information.
An explanation; a display.
