ex: Influenza and suspected influenza are FDA-approved indications for oseltamivir.
The first indication he meets by a dose of calomel, 1o to .30 gm., followed, if necessary, by magnesium sulphate in boiled water.

s.def: A mark or another symbol used to represent something.

ety: From Late Latin indicātor (“one who points out”), from Latin indicō (“point out”). By surface analysis, indicate + -or; see indicate.

s.def: Distinctive markings.
A preprinted marking on a mailpiece which shows that postage has been paid by the sender.

ex: They covered the infield with a tarp when it started to rain.

s.def: The region of the field roughly bounded by the wicket keeper, slips, gully, point, cover, mid off, mid on, midwicket and square leg.
The area inside a racetrack or running track.
ex: We left the carriage, bought programmes, and walked across the infield and then across the smooth thick turf of the course to the paddock.

s.def: A constrained scope or area.
ex: Let’s keep this problem in the infield.

s.def: (as a modifier, functioning as an adjective) Of an event, happening in the infield.
ex: Jones ran out an infield single.

s.def: To enclose (a piece of land); make a field of.
Toward or into the infield.

ety: From Middle English infiltrate (adjective), from Medieval Latin infiltrātus, from infiltrō.

s.def: to cause a fluid to pass through a substance by filtration
To surreptitiously penetrate, enter or gain access to.
ex: The spy infiltrated the high-tech company and stole many secrets.
Caithness was infiltrated with a palpable sense of being underimagined.

s.def: To cause to penetrate in this way.
ex: The agency infiltrated several spies into the company.

s.def: To pass through something by filtration.
To cause (a liquid) to pass through something by filtration.
To invade or penetrate a tissue or organ.
ex: High-grade tumors often infiltrate surrounding structures.
In certain conditions, immune cells may infiltrate into the cerebrospinal fluid.

s.def: To send (soldiers, spies, etc.) through gaps in the enemy line.
To move from a vein, remaining in the body.
Any undesirable substance or group of cells that has made its way into part of the body.
ex: One critical distinction to make is whether a focal corneal infiltrate is infected with bacteria or is a sterile immunologic response.
Extensive lumpy infiltrates with a tendency to caseate and to form fistulas with purulent secretions appear, mainly in the anogenital region.

ety: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinit and its etymon Latin īnfīnītus, from in- (“not”) + fīnis (“end”) + the perfect passive participle ending -ītus. By surface analysis, in- + finite. Doublet of infinito. Displaced native Old English unġeendodlīċ.

s.def: Indefinably large, countlessly great; immense.
ex: infinite riches in a little room
which infinite calamity shall cause to human life

s.def: Boundless, endless, without end or limits; innumerable.
ex: Great is our Lord, and of great power; his understanding is infinite.

s.def: Infinitely many.
Greater than any positive quantity or magnitude; limitless.
Having infinitely many elements.
Not limited by person or number.
Capable of endless repetition; said of certain forms of the canon, also called perpetual fugues, constructed so that their ends lead to their beginnings.
Infinitely many.
Something that is infinite in nature.
ex: Sooner Earth / Might go round Heaven, and the strait girth of Time / Inswathe the fulness of Eternity, / Than language grasp the infinite of Love.
Cautiously, Hobbes avoided asserting the equality of these infinites, and explicitly characterized the relation between them as non-inequality.

s.def: A combo that can be used repeatedly without interruption.
ex: […] prevents overpowered combos and infinites […]

s.def: A loop which continues indefinitely.

ety: From New Latin īnfīnītēsimus + -al. Displaced earlier coordinate term fluxion.

s.def: Incalculably, exceedingly, or immeasurably minute; vanishingly small.
ex: Do you ever get the feeling that you are but an infinitesimal speck, swallowed by the vastness of the universe and beyond?
"You will conceive a bunch of grapes," said he, "which are covered by some infinitesimal but noxious bacillus."

s.def: Of or pertaining to non-zero quantities whose magnitude is less than any positive rational number.
Very small.
A non-zero quantity whose magnitude is smaller than any positive number (by definition it is not a real number).
Something infinitesimally small.

ety: From Middle English infenitife (“without end, in perpetuity”), from Late Latin īnfīnītīvus (“unlimited, indefinite”), from Latin īnfīnītus (“unlimited, infinite”). By surface analysis, infinite + -ive.

s.def: A non-finite verb form considered neutral with respect to inflection; depending on language variously found used with auxiliary verbs, in subordinate clauses, or acting as a gerund, and often as the dictionary form.
The infinitive mood or mode (a grammatical mood).
ex: The MANNERS of acting, in grammar called modes or moods, are four; Infinitive, Imperative, Indicative, Subjunctive or Conjunctive.
There are four moods, the Infinitive, Imperative, Indicative, and Subjunctive. [...] the Infinitive is used to express a thing in a general manner.

s.def: A verbal noun formed from the infinitive of a verb.
Formed with the infinitive.
ex: INFINITIVE MOOD or MANNER. To Have, Avoir.
In English there are four moods:–1. The Infinitive Mood. 2. The Indicative Mood. 3. the Imperative Mood. 4. The Subjunctive Mood.

s.def: Unlimited; not bounded or restricted; undefined.

ety: From Old French infinité, from Latin infinitas (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + finis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tas.

s.def: The state or quality of being infinite or having no limit.
ex: Euclid proved the infinitude of primes.

ety: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinité, from Latin īnfīnitās (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + fīnis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tās. By surface analysis, infinite + -ity.

s.def: Endlessness, unlimitedness, absence of a beginning, end or limits to size.
ex: concept of infinity
The desert stretched out toward the horizon as if into infinity.

s.def: A number that has an infinite numerical value that cannot be counted.

A number which is very large compared to some characteristic number. For example, in optics, an object which is much further away than the focal length of a lens is said to be "at infinity", as the distance of the image from the lens varies very little as the distance increases further.
The symbol ∞.
An idealised point which is said to be approached by sequences of values whose magnitudes increase without bound.

ety: * The noun is from Middle English infirme, from Latin infirmus (“weak, feeble”). * The verb is from Latin īnfirmāre, from īnfirmus (“sick, weak, infirm”) + -ō.

s.def: Weak or ill, not in good health.
ex: He was infirm of body but still keen of mind, and though it looked like he couldn't walk across the room, he crushed me in debate.
[…] Here I stand your slave, A poor, infirm, weak, and despis’d old man.

s.def: Irresolute; weak of mind or will.
ex: Infirm of purpose! Give me the daggers: […]

s.def: Frail; unstable; insecure.

s.def: To contradict, to provide proof that something is not.

ety: From Medieval Latin infirmaria, from Latin infirmus.

s.def: A clinic or dispensary within another institution.

ety: Back-formation from Middle English infixed (“stuck in”), from Latin infixus, past participle of infigō (“to fasten in”).

Synonym of interfix.

ety: From Middle English inflammen, enflamen, enflaumen (“to set (something) on fire; to be on fire; (figurative) to enrage (someone); to become enraged; to incite (someone) to do evil; to inspire (someone); (medicine) to cause inflammation of (a body part)”), from Old French enflamer, enflammer (“to set (something) on fire, inflame; to be on fire; (figurative) to fuel (a debate, hatred, etc.)”) (modern French enflammer), from Latin inflammāre, the present active infinitive of inflammō (“to set (som…

s.def: To cause (something intangible, such as a dispute or violence, or hunger or thirst) to become more serious or worse; to aggravate, to exacerbate.

s.def: To increase (the price or quantity of something).
To burst into flames, to catch fire.
Of a person's body or body part: to feel abnormally or unusually hot; specifically (medicine), to be affected by inflammation.
To become very hot.

ety: From Middle French inflammable, from Medieval Latin īnflammābilis, from Latin īnflammāre (“to set on fire”), from in (“in, on”) + flamma (“flame”). By surface analysis, inflame + -able, literally “able to be inflamed”.

An instance of a plant beginning to flower.

ety: From Middle English ynneside; equivalent to in- + side. Compare German Innenseite (“inside”), Danish inderside (“inside”), Swedish insida (“inside”), Dutch binnenzijde (“inside”), German Low German Binnensied, Binnersied (“inside”), Saterland Frisian Binnersiede (“inside”).

ex: On a motorway, you should never pass another vehicle on the inside.

s.def: The side of a curved road, racetrack etc. that has the shorter arc length; the side of a racetrack nearer the interior of the course or some other point of reference.
ex: The car in front drifted wide on the bend, so I darted up the inside to take the lead.

s.def: The interior organs of the body, especially the guts.

ety: From Middle French insidieux, from Latin īnsidiōsus (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from īnsidiae (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + -ōsus, from īnsideō (“to sit in or on”), from in (“in, on”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

ety: From Latin insincerus.

ety: From Middle English inspiracioun, from Old French inspiration, from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem (nominative: īnspīrātiō), from Latin īnspīrātus (past participle of inspīrō). By surface analysis, inspire + -ation. Displaced native Old English onbryrdnes (literally “in-pricked-ness”).

s.def: A section of any footwear covering that part of the foot.
In horses, the hind leg from the ham to the pastern joint.

ety: Borrowed from Latin īnstīgātus, perfect passive participle of īnstīgō (“to instigate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To bring about by urging or encouraging.
ex: to instigate a riot
to instigate a change
In light of growing outrage against Mecham, House special counsel William French instigated an investigation into the governor's affairs last fall.

s.def: To goad or urge (a person) forward, especially to wicked actions.
ex: to instigate someone to a crime
he might instigate them to swear against the law of God

ety: From Latin īnstīgātor (“stimulator”), from īnstīgāre (present infinitive of īnstīgō (“to incite, set on, stimulate, rouse or urge”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp, to stab; to puncture; to goad”)) + -or (from -ō (suffix forming masculine agent nouns), from Proto-Indo-European *-h₃onh₂- (suffix forming nouns denoting authority or burden)); cognate with French instigateur. By surface analysis, instigate + -or.

s.def: A person who intentionally instigates, incites, or starts something, especially one that creates trouble.
ex: Near-synonyms: see Thesaurus:troublemaker
I love my lover. I do not want to be the instigator of anguish for her.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Latin stīlla Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin stīllō Latin instillōbor. English instill Borrowed from Latin instillō.

s.def: To cause a quality to become part of someone's nature.
ex: It is important to instill discipline in a child at an early age.

s.def: To pour in (medicine, for example) drop by drop.

ety: From Latin īnstīnctus, past participle of īnstinguō (“to incite, to instigate”), from in (“in, on”) + stinguō (“to prick”).

s.def: A natural or inherent impulse or behaviour.
ex: Many animals fear fire by instinct.
By a divine instinct, men's minds mistrust / Ensuing dangers.

s.def: An intuitive reaction not based on rational conscious thought.
ex: an instinct for order; to be modest by instinct
Debbie's instinct was to distrust John.

s.def: Imbued, charged (with something).
ex: The chariot of paternal deity […] / Itself instinct with spirit, but convoyed / By four cherubic shapes.
a noble performance, instinct with sound principle
It was a most Bedlamite catalogue of horrors, which, if true, made the wholesome moors a place instinct with tragedy.

ety: Etymology tree English instinct Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English instinctive From instinct + -ive.

s.def: Related to or prompted by instinct.
Driven by impulse, spontaneous and without thinking.
ex: When approached by a stranger, Jared clenched his fists in an instinctive manner.

ety: From instinct + -ual.

s.def: Of, relating to, or derived from instinct.

ety: From French institut, from Middle French, from Latin īnstitūtum.

s.def: An organization founded to promote a cause
ex: I work in a medical research institute.

s.def: An institution of learning; a college, especially for technical subjects
The building housing such an institution.
The act of instituting; institution.
ex: water sanctified by Christ's institute

s.def: That which is instituted, established, or fixed, such as a law, habit, or custom.
ex: They made a sort of institute and digest of anarchy.

s.def: The person to whom an estate is first given by destination or limitation.
ex: Substitution is the nomination of substituted heirs, who take place, failing the institute.

s.def: To begin or initiate (something); to found.
ex: He instituted the new policy of having children walk through a metal detector to enter school.
And haply institute / A course of learning and ingenious studies.

s.def: To train, instruct.
ex: If children were early instituted, knowledge would insensibly insinuate itself.

s.def: To invest with the spiritual charge of a benefice, or the care of souls.
ex: a writ issued to the bishop, to institute the clerk of that patron

s.def: To nominate; to appoint.
ex: We institute your Grace / To be our regent in these parts of France.

ety: From Middle English institucioun, from Old French institution, from Latin institūtiō, from instituō (“to set up”), from in- (“in, on”) + statuō (“to set up, establish”). Equivalent to institute + -ion.

s.def: established organisation
A long-established organization or type of organization, particularly one involved with education, public service, or charity work.
ex: The University of the South Pacific is the only internationally accredited institution of higher education in Oceania.
[…] these professors of Little Red Schoolhouse-education did not themselves remain in the isolated and handicapped little institution they glorify.
It is a common misconception […] that the American Mob began as an Italian institution transplanted directly from Sicily.

s.def: A custom or practice of a society or community.
ex: The institution of marriage is present in many cultures but its details vary widely across them.

s.def: The building or buildings which house such an organization.
ex: He's been in an institution since the crash.

s.def: A mental institution.
Any facility where people (especially those who are mentally or physically disabled or sick, or who are prisoners) are committed (confined), where their freedom to leave is restricted.
Any long established and respected place or business.
ex: Over time, the local pub has become something of an institution.

s.def: A person long established in a place, position, or field.
ex: She's not just any old scholar; she is an institution.

s.def: The act of instituting something.
ex: The institution of higher speed limits was a popular move but increased the severity of crashes.

s.def: The act by which a bishop commits a cure of souls to a priest.

ety: From institution + -al.

s.def: Of, pertaining to, characteristic of, or organized along the lines of an institution.
Instituted by authority.
ex: institutional ruling

s.def: Elementary; rudimentary.
Arising from the practice of an institution.
ex: There must be an unequivocal acceptance of the problem of institutional racism and its nature before it can be addressed

s.def: A client that is an organization rather than an individual.
A Chilean senator who is appointed by the president for a term of eight years.
A community where the majority of inhabitants work at an institution (as opposed to industry or trade), or one such inhabitant.
An institutionalized person.
ex: And I hope you can work it out where 'institutionals' can have rights too.
We have no groups that do not include ex-institutionals.

s.def: A person whose sense of self is based on institutionalized values and standards, as opposed to their tastes and impulses.
ex: For institutionals the self is revealed through adherence to a high standard, especially in spite of adverse conditions.
For the institutionals, hypocrisy consists of failing to live up to one's standards.

ety: Etymology tree English institution English -al English institutional Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English institutionalize From institutional + -ize.

s.def: To commit a person to confinement in an institution.
To establish as a normal practice.

ety: From institution + -ary.

s.def: Relating to an institution or institutions.
ex: […] Dr. Grant had brought on apoplexy and death, by three great institutionary dinners in one week, […]

s.def: Containing the first principles or doctrines; rudimentary.

ety: From Latin īnstitūtor. Compare French instituteur. By surface analysis, institute + -or.

s.def: One who institutes something.
ex: institutors of civil policy

s.def: One who educates; an instructor.
ex: The two great aims which every institutor of youth should mainly and intentionally drive at

s.def: A presbyter appointed by the bishop to institute a rector or assistant minister over a parish church.

ety: From Latin īnstrūctus, perfect passive participle of īnstruō (“I instruct; I arrange, furnish, or provide”).

s.def: To teach by giving instructions.
ex: Listen carefully when someone instructs you how to assemble the furniture.
Supply me with the habit and instruct me How I may formally in person bear me Like a true friar.
What a dishonour’s this, to me, to have so Dull a Father, that needs to be instructed in his Duty.

s.def: To tell (someone) what they must or should do.
ex: Usage note: "instruct" is less forceful than "order", but weightier than "advise"
The doctor instructed me to keep my arm immobilised and begin physiotherapy.
What, shall a child instruct you what to do?

s.def: To give (one's own lawyer) legal instructions as to how they should act in relation to a particular issue; thereby formally appointing them as one's own legal representative in relation to it.
ex: If you're not careful, I'm going to instruct a solicitor over this.

s.def: Instruction.
Arranged; furnished; provided.
ex: For he had neither ship, instruct with oares, Nor men to fetch him from those stranger shores.

s.def: Instructed; taught; enlightened.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Proto-Indo-European *ster- Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- Proto-Indo-European *strew- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *stréweti Proto-Italic *strowō Latin struō Latin īnstruō Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin īnstrūctiō Old French instruccion Middle English instruccioun English instruction From Middle English instruccio…

s.def: The act of instructing, teaching, or providing with information or knowledge.
ex: Students receive instruction in the arts and sciences.
Instruction will be provided on how to handle difficult customers.

s.def: An instance of the information or knowledge so furnished.
ex: If my instructions may be your guide.

s.def: An order or command.
A set of directions provided by a manufacturer for the users of a product or service.
The directions given by a client to their lawyer in relation to a particular legal matter, which govern the purpose and scope of their work.
ex: I cannot act until I have taken instructions from my client.

s.def: A single operation of a processor defined by an instruction set architecture.

ety: Etymology tree English instruct Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English instructive From instruct + -ive.

s.def: Conveying knowledge, information or instruction.
ex: Well, that was an instructive lesson.

s.def: A case in the Finnish and Estonian languages. It expresses the means or the instrument used to perform an action.

ety: From Middle English instrument, from Old French instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum (“an implement, tool”), From īnstruō (“build, construct; arrange”) + -mentum.

s.def: tool
A device used to produce music.
ex: The violinist was a master of her instrument.
But those who attack violists shouldn't throw resin. Once the ergonomic viola catches on what instrument will be immune?

s.def: A means or agency for achieving an aspect.
A measuring or displaying device.
ex: The instrument detected an increase in radioactivity.

s.def: A tool, implement used for manipulation or measurement.
ex: The dentist set down his tray of instruments.
The scientist recorded the temperature with a thermometer, but wished he had a more accurate instrument.

s.def: A legal document, such as a contract, deed, trust, mortgage, power, indenture, or will, or any of a class of negotiable ones (which can be exchanged for value or money).
ex: A bond indenture is the instrument that gives a bond its value.
Negotiable instruments are the foundation of the debt markets.

s.def: A person used as a mere tool for achieving a goal.
ex: Or useful serving man and instrument, / To any sovereign state.
The bold are but the instruments o' the wise.

s.def: To apply measuring devices.
ex: an instrumented test article

s.def: To devise, conceive, cook up, plan.
To perform upon an instrument; to prepare for an instrument.
ex: a sonata instrumented for orchestra

ety: From Middle English instrumental, instrumentale, from Medieval Latin īnstrūmentālis, equivalent to instrument + -al.

ex: the instrumental case

ex: instrumental music
an instrumental part

s.def: Serving as an instrument, medium, means, or agency.
Essential or central; of great importance or relevance.
ex: He was instrumental in conducting the business.

Few songwriters have been as instrumental in creating the mold for American music.

s.def: The instrumental case.
A composition written or performed without lyrics or singing, using a lead instrument to replace vocals.
A pause in the vocals of a song, usually occurring midway through, in which a musical instrument replaces the vocals.

A noun case used to express means or agency—and is generally indicated in English by by or with with the objective. Languages that use the instrumental case include Armenian, Serbo-Croatian, Czech, Dyirbal, Georgian, Latvian, Slovene, Polish, Ukrainian, Quechua, Russian, Assamese, Tamil, Turkish an…

s.def: The condition or quality of being instrumental; being useful; serving a purpose.

s.def: Something that is instrumental; an instrument.
ex: He spoke of the various instrumentalities which were now employed for the conversion of the world.
Delays and failures will only set her to casting about for new instrumentalities.
God works by instrumentalities, and he has wonderfully thus far interposed in keeping evils that I feared in abeyance.

s.def: A governmental organ with a specific purpose.
The property of being in the instrumental case.

ety: Etymology tree English instrument Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English instrumentation From instrument + -ation.

s.def: The act of using or adapting as an instrument; a series or combination of instruments.

The act or manner of playing upon musical instruments; performance.
ex: He had a wonderful instrumentation.

ex: The car's instrumentation included fuel, temperature, voltimeter and oil pressure gauges, along with a speedometer and tachometer.

s.def: Monitoring gauges for any machine, such as a reactor.
The dynamic analysis of a program's performance and behaviour, usually by injecting profiling code into it.
ex: bytecode instrumentation

s.def: The use of tools, instruments, or technical methods in the commission of a crime.

ety: From in- + subordinate, on model of French insubordonné.

s.def: Rebellious or defiant to authority; contumacious.
ex: I remembered with confusion my insubordinate and stealthy conduct, and when I saw where it had brought me […] I felt ashamed to look him in the face.

s.def: To rebel or defy authority.
ex: I think it's moral to insubordinate against a controlling boss.

s.def: A person who defies authority.

ety: Probably from Middle French insubstantiel, from Latin insubstantiālis, from in- + substantiālis. By surface analysis, in- + substantial.

s.def: Lacking substance; not real or strong.
ex: The bridge was insubstantial and would not safely carry a car.
By manipulating the flow of magic, Eragon quickly descended from the Ra'zac's lair—which the insubstantial wall of stone once again hid—to the ledge.

ety: From Late Middle English insufferable (“unbearably painful, intolerable”), and then either: * from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + sufferable, souffrable (“bearable, endurable, tolerable; allowable, permissible; able to or willing to bear hardship; forbearing, long-suffering; calm, self-restrained, slow to anger; capable of suffering”) (from Anglo-Norman sufferable, souffrable, and Old French souffrable, suffrable (“sufferable, tolerable”)); or * from Old French insouffrable (“which cannot be endu…

It became clear to me: guys who like Kafka—it’s never women—are insufferable.

ety: From Middle French insufficient, from Latin insufficiens. See also in- + sufficient.

s.def: An inadequate quantity of; not enough.
ex: Insufficient time is available to reflect on the problem.

s.def: A quantity (of something) that is less than is needed.
ex: Insufficient of the building remains to determine its age.

s.def: Not sufficient; of a type or kind that does not suffice, that does not satisfy requirements or needs.
ex: an insufficient amount
an insufficient degree
It is a necessary condition but an insufficient one.

s.def: Not sufficient; lacking competent power or ability; unqualified, unequal, unfit.

ety: First attested in 1670; borrowed from Latin īnsufflātus, perfect passive participle of īnsufflō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)) from in- + sufflō (“to blow on”). Cognate with French insuffler.

s.def: To breathe or blow into or on.
To treat by blowing a gas, vapor, or powder into a body cavity.
To inhale (a powder etc.).
To exhale upon baptismal water, or the one being baptised, as a ritual act.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsulāris (“of or belonging to an island”), from īnsula (“an island”), of uncertain origin.

s.def: Of or being, pertaining to, situated on, or resembling an island or islands.
ex: Near-synonym: islandic

s.def: Separate or isolated from the surroundings; having little regard for others opinions or prejudices; provincial.
ex: Near-synonym: peninsular

s.def: Having an inward-looking, standoffish, or withdrawn manner.
Relating to the insula in the brain.
Relating to insulin.

(often with a capital letter) Relating to the varieties of a language or languages spoken chiefly on islands. Insular Latin, Latin as it was spoken in Britain and Ireland. Insular Celtic, the Celtic languages of Britain, Ireland and also Brittany, as opposed to those spoken in mainland Europe other…
An islander.

ety: From Latin īnsula (“isle, island”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix) or from Late Latin īnsulātus (“made an island”), see etymology at -ate. Piecewise doublet of isolate.

s.def: To separate, detach, or isolate.
To separate a body or material from others, e.g. by non-conductors to prevent the transfer of electricity, heat, etc.
ex: Ceramic can be used to insulate power lines.

s.def: Of pollen or spores, with superficial ornamentation grouped in circular or polygonal areas separated by grooves.
ex: Among nonwinged grains, the sexine is rugulate, insulate, or microverrucate.
Pollen insulate when the elements are grouped in circular or polygonal areas separated by grooves.

ety: From insulate + -or.

s.def: A substance that does not transmit heat (thermal insulator), sound (acoustic insulator) or electricity (electrical insulator).
A non-conductive structure, coating or device that does not transmit sound, heat or electricity (see image)
ex: To isolate electrical wires from the pylons supporting them, one often uses glass insulators.

s.def: A person who installs insulation.

ety: From Latin īnsula (“island”) (named for the islets of Langerhans, where insulin is produced) + -in.

s.def: A polypeptide hormone that regulates carbohydrate metabolism (in various animals including humans).
ex: Mommy said that Grandma's diabetes happened because her body stopped making its own insulin.

s.def: Any exogenous preparation of this hormone for use as a medication.
ex: The advent of insulin in the mid-20th century changed the lives of millions of people with diabetes.

s.def: Any exogenous preparation of this hormone or its analogues for use as a medication.
ex: A: What kind of insulin do you take? B: I use basal-bolus therapy, which in my case involves glargine and lispro.

s.def: A pathological condition in which cells fail to respond normally to the hormone insulin; it is a form of, component of, and/or precursor of prediabetes (depending on nosologic viewpoint).

ety: The verb is derived from Middle French insulter (modern French insulter (“to insult”)) or its etymon Latin īnsultō (“to spring, leap or jump at or upon; to abuse, insult, revile, taunt”), the frequentative form of īnsiliō (“to bound; to leap in or upon”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’) + saliō (“to bound, jump, leap; to spring forth; to flow down”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“to spring”)). s.def: To assail, assault, or attack; (specifically, military) to carry out an assault, attack, or onset without preparation.
To behave in an obnoxious and superior manner (against or over someone).
To leap or trample upon.
Action or form of speech deliberately intended to be rude; (countable) a particular act or statement having this effect.
ex: To call you stupid would be an insult to stupid people!

s.def: Something that causes offence (for example, by being of an unacceptable quality).
ex: The way the orchestra performed tonight was an insult to my ears.

s.def: Something causing disease or injury to the body or bodily processes; the injury so caused.

s.def: An assault or attack; (specifically, military, obsolete) an assault, attack, or onset carried out without preparation.
An act of leaping upon.

ety: From Latin insuperabilis.

s.def: Impossible to achieve or overcome or be negotiated.

s.def: Overwhelming or insurmountable.
ex: For the first time I steadily reviewed the obstacles—and to consider them was at once to see they were insuperable.

ety: From Middle French insupportable, from Late Latin insupportabilis. See also in- + supportable.

s.def: That cannot be tolerated or endured.
ex: But in the prayer-room there was no furniture at all, the ground was of course sacred, and he found the smell of incense and sandalwood insupportable.

s.def: That cannot be supported; that cannot be demonstrated or proved. (of a statement, claim, argument, etc.)
ex: For the Conservatives, who came to power in 2006, to claim credit for more than two decades of dropping crime is as laughable as it is insupportable.

ety: From in- + suppressible.

s.def: That cannot be suppressed.
ex: It seemed as if the sense of public resentment had long been gathering strength unperceived, and now burst forth into insuppressible violence.

ety: From the older form ensurance, see also assurance. By surface analysis, insure + -ance.

s.def: A means of indemnity against a future occurrence of an uncertain event.
ex: The car was totalled, but fortunately I had insurance.

s.def: business
The business of providing insurance.
ex: After five years in banking, I switched to insurance.

s.def: Any attempt to forestall an unfavorable event.
ex: The sky was clear, but I took my umbrella for insurance.

s.def: A bet made after the deal, which pays off if the dealer has blackjack.
ex: I only take insurance if the count is right.

s.def: An insurance policy.
A company providing insurance policies; an insurer.
A company that provides insurance policies.
Receiving insurance policy-based compensation by deceitfully causing an event that, if it were accidental, would lead to a rightful claim for said compensation.
ex: Some people have committed insurance fraud by setting their houses on fire and claiming that the fire was an accident.

s.def: A legal document outlining a particular insurance cover for an insured entity for a given risk.
Something that protects or safeguards.

ety: First attested in c. 1440, as a variant of Middle English ensuren (from Anglo-Norman enseurer, itself from Old French en- + seür (“sure”), probably influenced by Old French asseürer (“to assure”)); took on its particular sense of "make safe against loss by payment of premiums" in 1635, replacing assure. Doublet of ensure.

s.def: To provide for compensation if some specified risk occurs. Often agreed by policy (contract) to offer financial compensation in case of an accident, theft or other undesirable event.
ex: I'm not insured against burglary.

s.def: To deal in such contracts; subscribe to a policy of insurance
Alternative spelling of ensure; to make sure or certain of; guarantee.
ex: The latest in automation equipment, combined with highly skilled craftsmen, insure the high quality of the Packard Clipper.

s.def: Covered by an insurance policy.

ety: Etymology tree English insure Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English insurer From insure + -er.

ex: Getting everybody to agree proved to be an insurmountable difficulty.
