ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Indo-European *-teros Proto-Indo-European *h₁énterosder. Latin *interus Latin intrābor. English intra- Proto-Germanic *natją Proto-West Germanic *nati Old English nett Middle English net English net English intranet From intra- + net.

s.def: A private computer network, typically one that uses the protocols of the Internet.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English transitive English intransitive From in- + transitive.

s.def: Not transitive: not having, or not taking, a direct object.
ex: The word "drink" is a transitive verb in "they drink wine", but an intransitive one in "they drink often."

s.def: Not transitive or passing further; kept; detained.

Of a set of dice: containing three dice A, B, and C, with the property that A rolls higher than B more than half the time, and B rolls higher than C more than half the time, but lacking the property that A rolls higher than C more than half the time. See intransitive dice and intransitive game.
An intransitive verb.
An action verb which does not take a direct object.
ex: In the English language, ‘sleep’ is an intransitive verb.
“‘Feel’ is an intransitive verb in your sentence and is modified by an adjective.”

s.def: The fluid pressure inside the eye.
A contraceptive device consisting of a spiral or similar shape of plastic or metal inserted through the vagina into the uterus in order to prevent the implantation of a fertilized egg.

ety: Etymology tree English intravenous Middle English -ly English -ly English intravenously From intravenous + -ly.

s.def: In an intravenous manner; by means of intravenous injection.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in- Proto-Indo-European *trep- Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin trepidus Latin intrepiduslbor. French intrépidebor. English intrepid From French intrépide, from Latin intrepidus, from in- (“not”) + trepidus (“anxious, nervous”).

s.def: Fearless; bold; brave.
ex: Fewer than 70 years earlier, the intrepid James Cook in his ship Resolution had been the first explorer to cross the Antarctic Circle.

ety: From intric(ate) + -acy.

s.def: The state or quality of being intricate or entangled.
ex: the intricacy of a knot
the intricacy of accounts
the intricacy of a cause in controversy

s.def: Perplexity.
Something which is intricate or complex.
ex: There are many intricacies in the plot of this novel.
With the most patient assiduity he peered into the intricacies of unrevealed structure. No object was too minute, none too large, for his attention.

ety: From Middle English intricat(e) (“entangled, intricate”), from Latin intrīcātus, perfect passive participle of intricō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: Having a great deal of fine detail or complexity.
ex: The architecture of this clock is very intricate.
From this point of vantage, we were able to gain an impression of the massive outlines of the main structure, and its intricate maze of girders.

s.def: Difficult to disentangle, puzzle apart, or resolve; enigmatic, obscure.
ex: His style of writing […] was […]fit to convey the most intricate business to the understanding […]with the utmost clearness.

s.def: To become enmeshed or entangled.
ex: […] washes off easily, without sticking or intricating into the wound.

s.def: To enmesh or entangle: to cause to intricate.
ex: But the British and French won't hear of that; they want to get their troops extricated and our ground troops intricated.

s.def: An intriguer.

ety: Borrowed from French intrigue, from Italian intricare, from Latin intrīcō (“to entangle, perplex, embarrass”). Doublet of intricate.

s.def: A complicated or clandestine plot or scheme intended to affect some purpose by secret artifice; conspiracy; stratagem; the practice of engaging in hidden schemes.
ex: His betrayal was the beginning of a complex intrigue intended to give him control of the company.
[…] lost in such a jungle of intrigues, pettifoggings, treacheries, diplomacies domestic and foreign […]

s.def: A desire to understand something; interest or fascination.
ex: Your idea has aroused my intrigue.

s.def: To conceive or carry out a secret plan intended to harm; to form a plot or scheme.
To arouse the interest of; to fascinate.
ex: Scenic illusions such as those caused by the haze, or the apparent diminution of scale where everything was enormous, intrigued Dutton.

s.def: To have clandestine or illicit intercourse.
To fill with artifice and duplicity; to complicate.
Causing a desire to know more; mysterious.
Involving oneself in secret plots or schemes.
ex: A book that does not sell us the powerful, intriguing women of Rome simply as poisoners, schemers, and femmes fatales […]

s.def: Having clandestine or illicit intercourse.

ety: Etymology tree English intrinsic Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al Middle English -ly Middle English -ally English -ally English intrinsically From intrinsic + -ally.

s.def: In an intrinsic manner; internally; essentially.
ex: What cannot be commoditized because it is intrinsically inaccessible to commodification?

s.def: Necessarily

ety: Clipping of introduction, from Latin intrōductiō (“lead-in, introduction”) – the abbreviation removes the second part of the compound; the first part ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁énteros (“inner, what is inside”). The demoscene sense comes from the fact that they were originally prepended to pirated copies of computer games.

s.def: An introduction.
The opening sequence at beginning of a film, television program, etc.
A small demo produced to promote one's demogroup or for a competition.
ex: If the rules specify that the DLLs' size will be added to the 64K limit, there's not a lot of space to code an intro.
Games, demos, intros. They were the same, this was the scene. The trend was that you cracked and made demos and intros.

s.def: To introduce.

ety: From Middle English introducen, from Old French introduire, from Latin intrōdūcō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁énteros (“inner, what is inside”) and *dewk-.

s.def: To cause (someone) to be acquainted (with someone else).
ex: Let me introduce you to my friends.

s.def: To bring (something) into practice.
ex: Wheeled transport was introduced long ago.

s.def: To make (something or someone) known, such as by formal announcement or recommendation.
ex: The senator plans to introduce the bill in the next session.
Let me introduce our guest speaker.

s.def: To add (something) to a system, a mixture, or a container.
ex: Various pollutants were introduced into the atmosphere.

ety: From Middle English introduccioun, introduccyon, borrowed from Old French introduction, itself a borrowing from Latin intrōdūctiōnem, accusative of Latin intrōdūctiō, from intrōdūcō. By surface analysis, intro- + Latin dūctiō or introduce + -tion.

s.def: The act or process of introducing.
ex: the introduction of a new product into the market

s.def: A means, such as a personal letter, of presenting one person to another.
ex: David was feeling groggy at his introduction to Sophie, and didn't remember her name.

s.def: An initial section of a book or article, which introduces the subject material.
ex: This book features a preface by a well-known botanist, and an introduction by the author's mentor at university.

s.def: A written or oral explanation of what constitutes the basis of an issue.
ex: ECON 101: introduction to economics

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin intrōductōrius, from Latin intrōductus.

s.def: Introducing; giving a preview, idea or foretaste of.
ex: He enrolled in an introductory wine-making course.

ety: PIE word *h₁én From Late Middle English introite (“act of entering in or into, entrance; place of entrance”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman introït, introïte (“introit”), or from its etymon Latin introitus (“act of entering in or into, entrance; passage; place of entrance; (figuratively) beginning, introduction, prelude”), from introeō (“to enter, go in”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns from verbs). Introeō is derived from intrō (“to enter, go into”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én…

s.def: A prayer, typically part of a psalm or other portion of the Bible, read or sung at the start of Mass while or immediately after the priest ascends to the altar.
Any piece of choral music, especially a setting of an anthem or a psalm, sung at the opening of a church service.
The action of entering or going in; an entrance.
An introduction.

ety: From intro-, by analogy with projection and interjection.

s.def: The process whereby the ideas of another are unconsciously incorporated into one's own psyche.
The process of forming a headmate who is in some way from another source.

ety: From Medieval Latin intrōmissiō, intrōmissiōn- (“introduction, admission; usurpation”), intro- (“into”) + missiō (“sending”), from Latin intrōmissus (“sent in, introduced, let in, admitted”), perfect passive participle of intrōmittō (“send in, let in”).

s.def: The state of being allowed to enter; admittance
The act of allowing to enter; admission
Putting one thing into another; introduction (into); insertion
Copulation: usually the first moment of initial entry of a penis into a vagina, mouth or anus.
An intermeddling with the affairs of another, either on legal grounds or without authority.

ety: From intragenic region.

s.def: A portion of a split gene that is included in pre-RNA transcripts but is removed during RNA processing and rapidly degraded.
ex: It is a medium-sized gene, then, interrupted by five longish introns.

ety: From Latin intrōspectus, past participle of intrōspiciō. By surface analysis, intro- + -spect.

s.def: To engage in introspection.
To look into.
To examine by means of type introspection.
ex: DynamicMBeanFacade uses Java's reflection API to introspect the managed resource and discover data type information for attributes.

ety: From Latin intrōspectiō, noun of action (with -iō) from past-participle (intrōspectus) stem of intrōspiciō (“to look into, look at, examine, observe attentively”), from intro- (“inward”) + speciō, spiciō (“to look at”). By surface analysis, introspect + -ion.

s.def: A looking inward; specifically, the act or process of self-examination, or inspection of one's own thoughts and feelings; the cognition which the mind has of its own acts and states.
Clipping of type introspection.
A sorting algorithm that begins with quicksort and switches to heapsort when the recursion depth exceeds a level based on (the logarithm of) the number of elements being sorted.

ety: From New Latin intrōversio, from intrōvertere (“to turn within”), from Classical Latin intro (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Equivalent to introvert + -sion or intro- + -version.

s.def: A turning inward
ex: ...their... Fastings, Prayings,... Introversions,... Humiliations, Mortifications...
The attending to the voice of Christ within you is what [mystics] term Introversion.
... Hamlet, who so perfectly typifies the introversion and complexity of modern thought as compared with ancient...

s.def: A turning inward, particularly
ex: This disease is sometimes produced by the introversion of the edge of the lower eyelid.

ety: From New Latin intrōvertere, from intro- (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung. By surface analysis, intro- + -vert.

s.def: An introverted person: one who is considered more thoughtful than social, with a personality more inwardly than outwardly directed; one who often prefers to have time in non-social situations.
ex: An Extravert can hardly conceive the necessity which compels the Introvert to conquer the world by means of a system.
All works of the imagination are conceived by men of the introvert type.
The introvert abstracts from the object and deals with it by concepts concentrating upon the inner world of thought.

s.def: An organ or other body part that is or can be turned inside out, especially an anterior portion of some annelid worms capable of retraction.
ex: Important distinctions which obtain amongst the various ‘introverts’ or intro- and e-versible tubes so frequently met with in animal bodies.
When a peanut worm feeds, it extends and waves its introvert so that the mouth at the tip wanders across the seabed.
The introvert is everted by hydraulic pressure exerted by contraction of body muscles on the coelomic fluid.

s.def: A reserved person.
Alternative form of introverted.
ex: They were noticeably more introvert, schizoid and desurgent in temperament.

s.def: To turn inwards.
ex: […] the Soul being straight, introverted […] into itself, and easily conforming to God's will and time […]
The less we look abroad, the more our ideas are introverted, and our habitual impressions... grow together into a kind of concrete substance.

ety: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).

s.def: To thrust oneself in; to come or enter without invitation, permission, or welcome; to encroach; to trespass.
ex: to intrude on families at unseasonable hours; to intrude on the lands of another
The noise of machinery intruded on an otherwise quiet morning.
Some thoughts rise and intrude upon us, while we shun them; others fly from us, when we would hold them.

s.def: To force in.

ety: Etymology tree English intrude Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English intruder From intrude + -er.

s.def: Someone who intrudes.
ex: All intruders will be shot!

ety: From Middle English intrusioun, from Old French intrusion, from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō, from Latin in- + trūdō.

s.def: Something that is intrusive or that has arisen from an act of intruding.
ex: I watched and felt intrusion upon the reigning terror of them

s.def: The forcible inclusion or entry of an external group or individual; the act of intruding.
ex: She viewed sales calls as an unwelcome intrusion.

ety: Back-formation from intrusion, + -ive.

s.def: Tending to intrude; doing that which is not welcome; interrupting or disturbing; entering without permission or welcome.
ex: Did it ever cross your mind that he might find all those questions you ask intrusive?

s.def: Of rocks: forced, while in a plastic or molten state, into the cavities or between the cracks or layers of other rocks.
epenthetic

Designating a type of collection in which each item keeps track of what collection it is in, rather than the more conventional approach of a collection keeping track of what items it contains. An intrusive collection does not "own" its contents and a single item can be part of multiple intrusive co…
ex: an intrusive linked list

s.def: An igneous rock that is forced, while molten, into cracks or between other layers of rock

ety: From in- + tube + -ate (verb-forming suffix). First appears c. 1612 in the publications of Simon Sturtevant.

s.def: To insert a tube into.
ex: The doctor is about to intubate the patient's trachea.

ety: Probably coined in 1880–1884 by Joseph O'Dwyer, M.D.; in widespread publication in 1887.

s.def: The introduction of a tube into an organ to keep it open, as into the larynx in cases of croup.

ety: From Middle French intuition, from Medieval Latin intuitiō (“a looking at, immediate cognition”), from Latin intueor (“to look at, consider”), from in- (“in, on”) + tueor (“to look, watch, guard, see, observe”). Equivalent to intuit + -ion.

s.def: Immediate cognition without the use of conscious rational processes.
A perceptive insight gained by the use of this faculty.

ety: Etymology tree English intuition Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English intuitionism From intuition + -ism.

s.def: An approach to mathematics/logic which avoids proof by contradiction, and which requires that, in order to prove that something exists, one must construct it.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French intuitif, from Medieval Latin intuitivus, from Latin intueri.

s.def: Spontaneous, without requiring conscious thought.
ex: The intuitive response turned out to be correct.

s.def: Easily understood or grasped by intuition.
ex: Designing software with an intuitive interface can be difficult.

s.def: Having a marked degree of intuition.
ex: I'm real intuitive, everyone is, we're just conditioned not to trust it.

ety: From Latin intumēscēns, present participle of intumescō (“rise, swell”), from tumescō (“become inflated”).

s.def: That becomes swollen, especially upon exposure to heat.
Any substance that swells on exposure to heat, thus increasing in volume and decreasing in density.
ex: Intumescents are used in some fire protection systems.

ety: Borrowed from French intussusception, or directly from Latin intussusceptiō, from intus (“within”) + susceptiō (“susception”).

s.def: The invagination of one portion of a tubular anatomical structure (especially intestines or blood vessels) within the next.
Absorption.

ety: From Latin inunctio, from inunctus, past participle of inungo (“anoint”), from in- + ungo (“anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“anoint”).

s.def: The anointing or rubbing in of oil or balm.

ety: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin inundātus, the perfect passive participle of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- + undō (“to overflow, wave”), from unda (“wave”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To cover with large amounts of water; to flood.
ex: The Dutch would sometimes inundate the land to hinder the Spanish army.

s.def: To overwhelm.
ex: The agency was inundated with phone calls.

ety: From Latin inurbānus. By surface analysis, in- + urbane.

s.def: uncivil; unpolished; rude
ex: Just would this be, and by no means inurbane

ety: From Middle English inuren, equivalent to in- + ure (“practise, exercise”).

s.def: To cause someone to become accustomed to something that requires prolonged or repeated tolerance of one or more unpleasantries.
ex: Matcht with as valiant men, and of as cleane a might, / As skilfull to commaund, and as inur’d to fight.
As Tom Paine warned, inuring us to lies lays the groundwork for many other evils.
This conflict produces a psychic numbing that inures us to the realities of being tracked, parsed, mined, and modified.

s.def: To take effect, to be operative.
To commit.
ex: He […] gan that ladie strongly to appele / Of many haynous crymes by her enured.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English urn English inurn From in- + urn.

s.def: To place (the remains of a person who has died) in an urn or other container.
To hold or contain (the remains of a person who has died).
ex: […] as the plough turns Some warlike relic from the sod, Whose mould the battle-ranks inurns,
Though you exist still, a mere form inurning The ashes of dead fires of thought and yearning,

ety: From Middle French inutile, from Latin inutilis. Philippine usage is likely from Tagalog inutil, from Spanish inútil, from the same source. By surface analysis, in- + utile.

s.def: useless; unprofitable.
ex: wormwood, and the like, […]dissipate and digest any inutile or excrementitious moisture which lieth in the flesh

s.def: useless (of a person); inept.

ety: From invade + -able.

s.def: Able to be invaded

ety: From Latin invādō (“enter, invade”).

s.def: To enter by force, usually in order to conquer.
ex: Argentinian troops invaded the Falkland Islands in 1982.

s.def: To move into.
ex: Under some circumstances police are allowed to invade a person's privacy.

s.def: To infest or overrun.
ex: The picnic was invaded by ants.

s.def: To attack; to infringe; to encroach on; to violate.
ex: The king invaded the rights of the people.

s.def: To make an unwelcome or uninvited visit or appearance, usually with an intent to cause trouble or some other unpleasant situation.

ety: Etymology tree English invade Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English invader From invade + -er.

s.def: One who invades a region.
ex: The underroot tendril! We are at fault for giving the invader a path to Lady Brianna.

s.def: An intruder (especially on someone's privacy).

ety: From Medieval Latin invāgīnātus, past participle of Medieval Latin invāgīnāre, from in- + vāgīna (“sheath”).

s.def: sheathed
Having one portion of a hollow organ drawn back within another portion.
To fold up or enclose into a sheath-like or pouch-like structure, either naturally or as part of a surgical procedure.
To turn or fold inwardly.
To fold inward to create a hollow space where none had existed, as with a gastrula forming from a blastula.

ety: Etymology tree English invaginate Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English -ion English invagination From invaginate + -ion.

s.def: The process where an anatomical part invaginates upon itself or into another structure.
One of the methods by which the various germ layers of the ovum are differentiated.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl̥h₁éh₁yeti Proto-Italic *walēō Latin valeō Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin validusder. Middle French validebor. English valid English invalid From in- + valid.

s.def: Not valid; not true, correct, acceptable, or appropriate.
ex: Your argument is invalid because it uses circular reasoning.
This invalid contract cannot be legally enforced.

s.def: sick person
Any person with a disability or illness.
A person who is confined to home or bed because of illness, disability or injury; one who is too sick or weak to care for themselves.
A disabled member of the armed forces; one unfit for active duty due to injury.
Suffering from disability or illness.
Intended for use by an invalid.
To exempt from (often military) duty because of injury or ill health.
ex: He was invalided home after the car crash.

s.def: To make invalid or affect with disease.

ety: First attested in 1649; borrowed from Middle French invalider, from invalide + -er. By surface analysis, in- + validate or invalid + -ate.

s.def: To make invalid (especially in to contract law)
ex: The circuit court judge's ruling was invalidated by a superior judge.

s.def: To make or declare (an argument, statement, or theory) unsound or erroneous; disprove.
ex: The multiplicity of moral opinions is an empirical fact and does not invalidate the contention that there is only one morality par excellence.

s.def: To render invalid; discredit.
ex: Telling an angry person to "calm down" can invalidate their feelings.

s.def: Made invalid.

ety: Etymology tree English invalid Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Latin -itāsder. Old French -itebor. Middle English -ite English -ity English invalidity From invalid + -ity.

s.def: The state of being invalid; lack of validity.

ety: From in- + valuable (compare priceless). Piecewise doublet of unvaluable.

s.def: Having great or incalculable value.
Not valuable; valueless; worthless.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English variable English invariable From in- + variable. Piecewise doublet of unvariable.

s.def: Not variable; unalterable; uniform; always having the same value.
ex: Physical laws which are invariable.

s.def: Constant.
That cannot undergo inflection, conjugation or declension.
ex: The French adjective marron ‘brown’ is invariable: it does not take the usual s in the plural.

s.def: Something that does not vary; a constant.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English variant English invariant From in- + variant.

s.def: Not varying; constant.
Unaffected by a specified operation, especially by a transformation.
Neither covariant nor contravariant.
An invariant quantity, function etc.
ex: In the present paper this criterion is reformulated in terms of pseudotensorial invariants of the form..

s.def: Ellipsis of class invariant.

ety: From Middle French invasion, from Late Latin invāsiōnem, accusative of invāsiō.

s.def: A military action consisting of a large armed force of one geopolitical entity entering territory controlled by another such entity, generally with the objective of conquering territory or altering the established government.
ex: The invasion and armed suppression, on one occasion after another, of nations seeking to be free was quite consistent with Lenin's views.

s.def: The entry without consent of an individual or group into an area where they are not wanted.
ex: an invasion of mobile phones
an invasion of bees
an invasion of foreign tourists

s.def: The spread of cancer cells, bacteria and such to the organism.
The breaching of the skin barrier.

Any species that has been introduced to an environment where it is not native, and that has since become a nuisance through rapid spread and increase in numbers, often to the detriment of native species.

ety: From Middle French invective, from Medieval Latin invectiva (“abusive speech”), from Latin invectīvus, from invectus, perfect passive participle of invehō (“bring in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). See vehicle, and compare with inveigh.

s.def: An expression which inveighs or rails against a person.
A severe or violent censure or reproach.
Something spoken or written, intended to cast shame, disgrace, censure, or reproach on another.
A harsh or reproachful accusation.
ex: Politics can raise invective to a low art.

s.def: Characterized by invection or railing.
ex: Tom's speeches became diatribes — each more invective than the last.

ety: Borrowed from Latin invehō (“bring in, carry in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). Compare vehicle, invective.

s.def: To complain loudly, to give voice to one's censure or criticism
ex: Only last week, three aggressively written pamphlets crossed my desk inveighing against the euro.

s.def: To draw in or away; to entice, inveigle.
ex: He is a Spirit, that inveighs away a Man from himself, undertakes great Matters for him, and after fells him for a Slave.

ety: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman enveugler, alteration of aveugler (“to blind, to delude”), from Old French avogle (“without eyes”), from Late Latin ab oculīs (“without eyes”, literally “away from the eyes”). The in- might be by analogy to variation between a- and en- in other French words, which was then latinised into in-. For the pronunciation with /iː/, compare the development of people; that with /eɪ/ is presumably a spelling pronunciation.

s.def: To convert, convince, or win over with flattery or wiles.
To obtain through guile or cunning.
ex: He inveigled an introduction to my sister from me.

s.def: To fool, to delude, to blind in judgement.
To ensnare, to entangle.

ety: From Middle English inventen, borrowed from Old French inventer, from Latin inventus, perfect passive participle of inveniō (“come upon, meet with, find, discover”), from in (“in, on”) + veniō (“come”); see venture. Compare advent, covent, event, prevent, etc. Displaced native Old English āþenċan (literally “to think out”).

s.def: To design a new process or mechanism.
ex: After weeks of hard work, I invented a new way to alphabetize matchbooks.

s.def: To create something fictional for a particular purpose.
ex: I knew I had to invent an excuse, and quickly.
We need a name to put in this form, so let's just invent one.

s.def: To come upon; to find; to discover.
ex: Far off he wonders, what them makes so glad, / If Bacchus merry fruit they did inuent [...].

ety: From Middle English invencion, invencioun, from Latin inventiō either directly or via Middle French invencion, from Latin invenīre (“to discover, find, invent”), from in- (“in-: in, into”) + venīre (“to come”). Doublet of inventio. By surface analysis, invent + -ion. Displaced native Old English orþanc.

s.def: Something invented.
ex: My new invention will let you alphabetize your matchbook collection in half the usual time.
I’m afraid there was no burglar. It was all the housekeeper’s invention.
Warren Sheffield is telephoning Rose long distance at half past six. […] Personally, I wouldn't marry a man who proposed to me over an invention.

s.def: The act of inventing.
ex: The invention of the printing press was probably the most significant innovation of the medieval ages.

s.def: The capacity to invent.
ex: It took quite a bit of invention to come up with a plan, but we did it.

s.def: A small, self-contained composition, particularly those in J.S. Bach’s Two- and Three-part Inventions.
ex: I particularly like the inventions in C-minor.

s.def: The act of discovering or finding; the act of finding out; discovery.
ex: That judicial method which serveth best for the invention of truth.

der: necessity is the mother of invention

ety: From Middle English inventif, inventyfe, borrowed from Old French inventif, borrowed from Medieval Latin inventivus. By surface analysis, invent + -ive.

s.def: Of, or relating to invention; pertaining to the act of devising new mechanisms or processes.
ex: an inventive pursuit

s.def: Possessed of a particular capacity for the design of new mechanisms or processes, creative or skilful at inventing.
ex: an inventive fellow

s.def: Purposely fictive.
ex: an inventive story

ety: Borrowed from Latin inventor. By surface analysis, invent + -or.

s.def: One who invents, either as a hobby or as an occupation.
ex: Thomas Edison was the inventor of the phonograph.
The young inventor received a patent for her design.

ety: From Middle English inventorie, from Medieval Latin inventōrium, alteration of Late Latin inventārium, from Latin inveniō (“to find out”).

s.def: The stock of an item on hand at a particular location or business.
ex: Due to an undersized inventory at the Boston outlet, customers had to travel to Providence to find the item.

s.def: A detailed list of all of the items on hand.
ex: The inventory included several items that one wouldn't normally think to find at a cheese shop.

s.def: The process of producing or updating such a list.
ex: This month's inventory took nearly three days.

s.def: A space containing the items available to a character, especially in a video game, for immediate use.
ex: You can't get through the underground tunnel if there are more than three items in your inventory.
From the inventory tab you have the option to use the mobile phone or check out gadgets you have collected.

s.def: The total set of a (specified) linguistic feature (within a language etc.)
ex: Germanic languages have a marked tendency towards large vocalic inventories.

s.def: To take stock of the resources or items on hand; to produce an inventory.
ex: The main job of the night shift was to inventory the store, and restock when necessary.
‘Now,’ said Jethro, ‘we’re inventorying all the stock today, do you want to lend a hand?’

ety: From in- + veracity.

s.def: A lack of veracity
untruth, falsehood

ety: Recorded since 1440, from Latin inversus, the past participle of invertere (“to invert”), itself from in- (“against, in”) + vertere (“to turn”).

s.def: Opposite in effect, nature or order.
Reverse, opposite in order.
Inverted; having a position or mode of attachment the reverse of that which is usual.
Having the properties of an inverse; said with reference to any two operations, which, when both are performed in succession upon any quantity, reproduce that quantity.
ex: Multiplication is the inverse operation to division.

s.def: Whose every element has an inverse (morphism which is both a left inverse and a right inverse).
That has the property of being an inverse (the result of a circle inversion of a given point or geometrical figure); that is constructed by circle inversion.
ex: A circle inversion maps a given generalized circle to its inverse generalized circle.

s.def: The result of an inversion
ex: The inverse P‘ of a point P is the point on a ray from the center O through P such that OP × OP‘ = r² or the set of all such points.

s.def: A second element which negates a first; in a binary operation, the element for which the binary operation—when applied to both it and an initially given element—yields the operation's identity element, specifically:
ex: The multiplicative inverse of x is x⁻¹, as x×x⁻¹=1, as 1 the multiplicative identity element.

s.def: A morphism which is both a left inverse and a right inverse.
The winning of the coup in a game of rouge et noir by a card of a color different from that first dealt; the area of the table reserved for bets upon such an outcome.
ex: The tailleur never mentions the words ‘Black’ or ‘Inverse’, but always says that Red wins or Red loses, and that the colour wins or the colour loses.

ety: From Latin inversiōnem.

s.def: The action of inverting.
The reversal of an interval; the move of one pitch in an interval up or down an octave.
The position of a chord which has a note other than the root as its bass note.
The flipping of a melody or contrapuntal line so that high notes become low and vice versa; the reversal of a pitch contour.
A segment of DNA in the context of a chromosome that is reversed in orientation relative to a reference karyotype or genome.

Deviation from standard word order, as for example by putting the predicate before the subject. It takes place in questions with auxiliary verbs; in normal, affirmative clauses beginning with a negative particle, for the purpose of emphasis; and in other rhetorical devices or unusual situations.
The act of being in an inverted state; being upside down, inside out, or in a reverse sequence.
A situation where air temperature increases with altitude (the ground being colder than the surrounding air).
A section of a roller coaster where passengers are temporarily turned upside down.
An operation on a group, analogous to negation.

ety: From Middle French invertir.

s.def: To turn (something) upside down or inside out; to place in a contrary order or direction; to make (something) the opposite of it.
ex: to invert a cup, the order of words, rules of justice, etc.
ob-: used as a prefix inverts the term affixed.

s.def: To move (the root note of a chord) up or down an octave, resulting in a change in pitch.
To undergo inversion, as sugar.
To divert; to convert to a wrong use.
To turn (the foot) inwards.
An inverted arch (as in a sewer).
The base of a tunnel on which the road or railway may be laid and used when construction is through unstable ground. It may be flat or form a continuous curve with the tunnel arch.
The lowest point inside a pipe at a certain point.
An elevation of a pipe at a certain point along the pipe.
A skateboarding and snowboarding trick where the skater grabs the board and plants a hand on the coping so as to balance upside-down on the lip of a ramp.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English vertebrate English invertebrate From in- + vertebrate.

s.def: An animal without vertebrae (i.e., without a backbone).
A spineless person; a coward.
Without a backbone: without vertebrae.
Cowardly, uncourageous; lacking character.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French investir or Medieval Latin investire, from Latin investio (“to clothe, cover”), from in- (“in, on”) + vestio (“to clothe, dress”), from vestis (“clothing”); see vest. The sense “to spend money etc.” probably via Italian investire, of the same root.

s.def: To commit money or capital in the hope of financial gain.
To spend money, time, or energy on something, especially for some benefit or purpose; used with in.
ex: We'd like to thank all the contributors who have invested countless hours into this event.
We did not spend. We invested. [CEO Jeff Housenbold: He's learning!] I invest. Yes, I invested. I invested in a city for the contestants.

s.def: To clothe or wrap (with garments).
ex: He was but shabbily apparelled in faded jacket and patched trowsers; a rag of a black handkerchief investing his neck.

s.def: To put on (clothing).
ex: Cannot find one this girdle to invest!

s.def: To envelop, wrap, cover.
ex: Night / Invests the Sea, and wished Morn delayes

s.def: To ceremonially install someone in some office.
To formally give (someone) some power or authority.
ex: I do invest you jointly with my power.

s.def: To formally give (power or authority).
To surround, accompany, or attend.
To lay siege to.
ex: to invest a town

ety: Recorded since circa 1510, a back-formation from investigation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin investīgātiō (“a searching into”), from investīgātus, the perfect passive participle of investīgō, equivalent to in- + vestigate. Displaced native Old English undersēċan (literally “to search under or between”).

s.def: To inquire into or study in order to ascertain facts or information.
ex: to investigate the causes of natural phenomena
He was asked to investigate a robbery.
We investigated the presence of CNM in ornithophagous ticks from migrating birds.

s.def: To examine, look into, or scrutinize in order to discover something hidden or secret.
ex: to investigate an unsolved murder

s.def: To conduct an inquiry or examination.
ex: "Why don't you investigate?" he demanded. And investigate I did.

ety: From Middle English investigacioun, from Old French investigacion, from Latin investigatio. Morphologically investigate + -ion.

s.def: The act of investigating; the process of inquiring into or following up; research, especially patient or thorough inquiry or examination
ex: The investigation into the crime has led to various leads as well as plenty of dead ends.
Despite thorough investigation, the perpetrator of the attacks remains unknown.
carry out an investigation

ety: Attested in the mid‐16th century; from Latin investigator, from investigare, equivalent to investigate + -or.

s.def: One who investigates.

ety: From Middle French investiture, from Medieval Latin investītūra, from investīre (“to clothe”).

s.def: The act of investing, as with possession or power; formal bestowal or presentation of a possessory or prescriptive right.
The formal installation or, generally, the appointment of a bishop, or (uncountable) bishops in general.
That which invests or clothes; covering; vestment.
The parliamentary vote required to inaugurate the Prime Minister of Spain.
ex: The Spanish constitution dictates that the king is obliged to dissolve the legislative body two months after the first failed investiture vote.

ety: Etymology tree English invest Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English investment From invest + -ment.

s.def: A placement of capital in expectation of deriving income or profit from its use or appreciation.
ex: An investment in ink, paper, and steel pens.

s.def: The act of investing, or state of being invested.
ex: Giving your children a good education is a wise long-term investment.

s.def: A vestment.
ex: Whose white investments figure innocence.

s.def: The act of surrounding, blocking up, or besieging by an armed force, or the state of being so surrounded.
ex: the investment of the fort

s.def: A mixture of silica sand and plaster which, by surrounding a wax pattern, creates a negative mold of the form used for casting, among other metals, bronze.

ety: Etymology tree English invest Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -tor Latin -ātor Old French -eorbor. Middle English -our ▲ Latin -torlbor. English -or English investor From invest + -or.

s.def: A person who invests money in order to make a profit.

ety: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1574; borrowed from Latin inveterātus (“of long standing, chronic”), perfect passive participle of inveterō and participial adjective (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, into”) + veterō (“to age”), from vetus, veteris (“old”). Cognate with Italian inveterato, French invétéré. By surface analysis, in- (“not, opposite”) + veterate.

s.def: Firmly established from having been around for a long time; of long standing.
ex: Near-synonyms: deep-rooted, ingrained, ineradicable, indelible, radicated, chronic, permanent
an inveterate disease
an inveterate habit

s.def: Having had a habit (usually a bad habit) for a long time.
ex: Near-synonyms: hardened, chronic, dyed-in-the-wool
an inveterate idler; an inveterate gambler; an inveterate smoker
an inveterate traveller

s.def: Malignant; virulent; spiteful.
ex: A man of mild manners can form no idea of inveterate revenge or cruelty[…]

s.def: To fix and settle after a long time; to entrench.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English viable English inviable From in- + viable.

s.def: Synonym of nonviable.

ety: Borrowed from Latin invidiōsus, from invidia (“envy, ill will”), from in- (“upon”) + videō (“to see”); the meaning developed from “look back at” to “look askance at” to “envy.” Doublet of envious, from Old French.

s.def: Causing ill will, envy, or offense.
ex: ‘I didn’t make use of the word in any invidious sense, ma’am,’ replied Mr. Benjamin Allen, growing somewhat uneasy on his own account.
I should be very reluctant, as head of His Majesty's Government, to place such an invidious responsibility upon a British officer.

s.def: Offensively or unfairly discriminating.
ex: But the rich man—not to make any invidious comparison—is always sold to the institution which makes him rich.

s.def: Envious, jealous.
Detestable, hateful, or odious. (Often used in cases of perceived unfairness, or when facing a difficult situation or choice — especially in the phrase invidious position.)

ety: First attested in 1646; borrowed from New Latin invigōrātus, perfect passive participle of invigōrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + vigor + -ate.

s.def: To impart vigor, strength, or vitality to.
ex: Exercise is invigorating.

s.def: To heighten or intensify.
To give life or energy to.
ex: The cold water invigorated him.

s.def: To make lively.
Invigorated, filled with vigour.
ex: The soldiers from the earth Leap up invigorate, […]

ety: From Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”), from in- (“not”) + vincibilis (“conquerable”), from vincere (“to conquer”).

s.def: Impossible to defeat, destroy, or kill; too powerful to be defeated or overcome.
ex: Nothing in this world could / Ever bring them down / Yeah, they're invincible / And she's just in the background
I'm unstoppable / I'm a Porsche with no brakes / I'm invincible / Yeah, I win every single game

s.def: Someone or something that cannot be defeated, destroyed, or killed.

ety: From Middle French inviolable, from Latin inviolābilis (“untouchable”), from violō (“violate”). Equivalent to in- + violable. Piecewise doublet of unviolable.

s.def: Not violable; not to be infringed.
ex: One more request, and I am lost, / If you its earnest prayer deny ; / It is, that you preserve the most / Inviolable secrecy / As to my plan.
"Now, Mr. Jones, having obtained your promise of inviolable secrecy, I come down to the essential point."

s.def: Not susceptible to violence, or of being profaned, corrupted, or dishonoured.
Incapable of being injured or invaded; indestructible.

ety: From Middle English inviolat, inviolate, from Latin inviolātus. By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + violate (adjective).

s.def: Not violated; free from violation or hurt of any kind; secure against violation or impairment.
ex: His fortune of arms was still inviolate.

s.def: Incorruptible.
ex: inviolate truth
There chaste Alceste lives inviolate.

ety: From Middle French invisibilité, from Latin invisibilitas.

s.def: The state of being invisible.
That which is invisible.

ety: From Middle English invisible, from Old French invisible, from Late Latin invīsibilis. Displaced native Old English unġesewenlīċ. Morphologically in- + visible. Piecewise doublet of unvisible.

s.def: Unable to be seen; out of sight; not visible.
Not appearing on the surface.
ex: The physical covering of this image limited the Christians’ view, rendering the image invisible on all but a few occasions.

s.def: Apparently, but not actually, offline.
ex: I went invisible so that my ex-girlfriend wouldn't send me instant messages.

s.def: That is ignored by a person.
To make invisible, to invisiblize.
An invisible person or thing; specifically, God, the Supreme Being.
A Rosicrucian; so called because avoiding declaration of his craft.
One of those (as in the 16th century) who denied the visibility of the church.
ex: Invisibles. Heretics who denied the visibility of the Church

ety: Coined by Scottish economist and philosopher Adam Smith in 1776 in his book The Wealth of Nations.

s.def: A metaphor for the principle that in a free market, an individual pursuing his own self-interest also tends to promote the good of his community as a whole.
ex: In short, Smith understood that the invisible hand is often benign, but not always.
Aha, they say, but extreme wealth is good for all of us. All will be uplifted by their god’s invisible hand. […]

ety: From Middle English invitacioun, ynvytacioun, from Latin invītātio, reinforced by Middle French invitation. By surface analysis, invite + -ation. Displaced native Middle English lathinge from Old English laþung (see dialectal English lathing).

s.def: The act of inviting; solicitation; the requesting of a person's company.
ex: an invitation to a party, to a dinner, or to visit a friend

s.def: A document or verbal message conveying an invitation.
ex: We need to print off fifty invitations for the party.

s.def: Allurement; enticement.
A line that is intentionally left open to encourage the opponent to attack.
The brief exhortation introducing the confession in the Anglican communion-office.
A bid that tells one's partner that game or slam is likely if their hand is at the strong end of what they have indicated.
ex: I assume also that opener would have shown no interest in slam by either bidding 4NT or 50 after the slam invitation of 46.

ety: From Latin invitatorius.

s.def: Of or pertaining to an invitation
A psalm sung, as an invitation to prayer, at the beginning of some services

ety: From Middle French inviter, from Latin invītō. Displaced native English lathe.

s.def: To ask for the presence or participation of someone or something.
ex: We invited our friends round for dinner.
A Nimph is marryed to a Fay, Great preparations for the Day, All Rites of Nuptials they recite you, To the Brydall and inuite you.

s.def: To request formally.
ex: I invite you all to be seated.
I always invite criticism of my essays.

s.def: To encourage.
ex: Wearing that skimpy dress, you are bound to invite attention.
The refusal to maintain such a navy would invite trouble, and if trouble came would insure disaster.
"Blindness invites confidence," replied Carrados. "We are out of the running—human rivalry ceases to exist. […]"

s.def: To allure; to draw to; to tempt to come; to induce by pleasure or hope; to attract.
ex: to inveigle and invite th' unwary sense
shady groves, that easy sleep invite
There no delusive hope invites despair.

s.def: An invitation.

ety: From invite + -er.

s.def: Someone who invites.

ety: From Middle English invocacioun, from Old French invocacion, from Latin invocatio, invocationem. Equivalent to invoke + -ation.

s.def: The act or form of calling for the assistance or presence of some superior being, especially prayer offered to a divine being.
A call or summons, especially a judicial call, demand, or order.
ex: the invocation of papers or evidence into court

s.def: An act of invoking or claiming a legal right.
The act of invoking, such as a function call.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French envois pl, plural of envoi, from the verb envoyer (“to send”). See also envoy.

s.def: A bill; a commercial document issued by a seller to a buyer indicating the products, quantities and agreed prices for products or services that the seller has already provided the buyer with. An invoice indicates that, unless paid in advance, payment is due by the buyer to the seller, according to…
ex: I've already rendered the invoices for payment.

s.def: The lot or set of goods as shipped or received.
ex: The merchant receives a large invoice of goods.

s.def: The price which a seller or dealer pays the manufacturer for goods to be sold.
A kind of receipt that serves as a tax document and sometimes also as a lottery ticket.
To bill; to issue an invoice to.
ex: I will invoice my supplier tomorrow.

s.def: To make an invoice for (goods or services).

ety: From Middle English *invoken, envoken, borrowed from Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre (“to call upon”), itself from in- + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of invocate.

s.def: To call upon (a person, a god) for help, assistance or guidance.
To solicit, petition for, appeal to a favorable attitude.
ex: The envoy invoked the King of Kings's magnanimity to reduce his province's tribute after another drought.
Whatever the pressures that have invoked the Minister's diktat, the outcome is Gilbertian.

s.def: To call another ship.
To call to mind (something) for some purpose.
ex: It is easier to invoke or to deplore democracy than to say exactly what it is.

s.def: To appeal for validation to a (notably cited) authority.
ex: In certain Christian circles, invoking the Bible constitutes irrefutable proof.
He invoked cadaveric poisoning as the reason for the high death rate among priests and monks […]

s.def: To conjure up with incantations.
ex: This satanist ritual invokes Beelzebub.

s.def: To bring about as an inevitable consequence.
ex: Blasphemy is taboo as it may invoke divine wrath.

s.def: To cause (a program or subroutine) to execute.
ex: Interactive programs let the users enter choices and invoke the corresponding routines.
[…]the selling price and cost of a particular item are derived by the system through a table lookup and assigned to the item at invoking time.
C++ lets you invoke an operator function either by calling the function or by using the overloaded operator with its usual syntax.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- Middle English voluntarie English voluntary English involuntary From in- + voluntary, from Late Latin involontarius, from in + volontarius.

s.def: Without intention; unintentional.
Not voluntary or willing; contrary or opposed to explicit will or desire; unwilling.
ex: He found himself the involuntary witness in the trial.

s.def: A muscle that is not controlled by individual volition, e.g., cardiac muscle and smooth muscle.

ety: Borrowed from Latin involutus.

s.def: Difficult to understand; complicated.
ex: These vulgar, pleasure-seeking people, so frank and clamorous, were too uninhibited for his shielded and involuted life.

s.def: Having the edges rolled with the adaxial side outward.
ex: Furthermore, the free anterior margin of the lobule is arched toward the lobe and is often involute[…]

s.def: Having a complex pattern of coils in which younger whorls only partly surround older ones.
Turned inward at the margin, like the exterior lip of the shells of species in genus Cypraea.
Rolled inward spirally.
To roll or curl inwards.
A curve that cuts all tangents of another curve at right angles; traced by a point on a string that unwinds from a curved object.

ety: From Latin involūtiō, from involvō.

s.def: Entanglement; a spiralling inwards; intricacy.
ex: […]usually his attention was diverted from her feet by her shrieks of laughter and the astounding involutions of her huge brown-yellow frame.
‘Gomez,’ said the mortician, ‘is an expert only on the involutions of his own rectum.’

s.def: A complicated grammatical construction.
An endofunction whose square is equal to the identity function; a function equal to its inverse.
ex: Involutions have the property that they are their own inverses.

s.def: The shrinking of an organ (such as the uterus) to a former size.
The regressive changes in the body occurring with old age.
A power: the result of raising one number to the power of another.
A cessation of development or progress involving intense inner competition.
A state of increased competition for limited resources, requiring great effort to stay ahead.
The migration of a cell layer inward, sliding over an outer layer of cells. It occurs at gastrulation during embryogenesis.

ety: PIE word *h₁én From Late Middle English involven (“to cloud; to encumber; to envelop, surround; to ponder (something); (reflexive) to concern (oneself) with something”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French involver, envoudre, or from its etymon Latin involvere, the present active infinitive of Latin involvō (“to roll to or upon something; to roll about; to coil or curl up; to cover; to envelop, wrap up; to overwhelm”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’) + volvō (“to roll; to…

s.def: To have (something) as a component or a related part; to comprise, to include.
ex: My job involves forecasting economic trends.

s.def: To cause or engage (someone or something) to become connected or implicated, or to participate, in some activity or situation.
ex: By involving herself in her local community, Mary met lots of people and also helped make it a nicer place to live.
How can we involve the audience more during the show?
I don’t want to involve him in my personal affairs.

s.def: To entangle, intertwine, or mingle (something with one or more other things, or several things together); especially, to entangle (someone or something) in a confusing or troublesome situation.
ex: to involve a person in debt or misery
[O]ld Œdipus / Would be amazd, and take it in foule snufs / That such Cymerian darknes should involve / A quaint conceit that he could not resolve.
Our misfortunes vvere involved together— […]

s.def: To cover or envelop (something) completely; to hide, to surround.
ex: to involve in darkness or obscurity
Or I saw / Fog only, the great tawny weltering fog, / Involve the passive city, strangle it / Alive, and draw it off into the void, […]

s.def: To form (something) into a coil or spiral, or into folds; to entwine, to fold up, to roll, to wind round.
ex: [S]ome of Serpent kinde / Wondrous in length and corpulence involv'd / Thir Snakie foulds, and added wings.

s.def: To make (something) intricate; to complicate.
To multiply (a number) by itself a given number of times; to raise to any assigned power.
ex: a quantity involved to the third or fourth power

ety: From involve + -ed.

s.def: Complicated.
ex: He related an involved story about every ancestor since 1895.
Miss Price told him a long, involved story, which made out that Mrs. Otter, a humdrum and respectable little person, had scabrous intrigues.
E-commerce has turned even the laying of a floor into a fiendishly involved business.

s.def: Associated with others, be a participant or make someone be a participant (in a crime, process, etc.)
ex: The people involved in the project for three years.
He got/was involved in a bar fight.
When the family wrapped up my father's will, no one tried to make me feel involved.

s.def: Having an affair with someone.
simple past and past participle of involve
ex: The explanation involved potatoes, squirrels, and race cars.

ety: Etymology tree English involve Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English involvement From involve + -ment.

s.def: The act of involving, or the state of being involved.

ety: From Middle French invulnérable, from Latin invulnerābilis, from vulnerābilis, from vulnerō (“to wound”), from vulnus (“wound”), equivalent to in- + vulnerable.

s.def: Incapable of being injured; not vulnerable.
ex: His gaze went to Hirken, who stood gloating behind invulnerable transparisteel.

s.def: Unanswerable; irrefutable.
ex: an invulnerable argument

ety: From Middle English inward, from Old English inweard, corresponding to in + -ward.

s.def: Situated on the inside; that is within, inner; belonging to the inside.
Not superficially obvious, inner, not expressed, especially relating to mental or spiritual faculties as opposed to external ones.
Moving or tending toward the inside.
Not directed toward the outside world, and thus quiet or indistinct.
Internal to a particular place or country; not foreign, domestic.
Secret, private, kept hidden.
Coming from one’s inmost or sincerest feelings; heartfelt, earnest.
Intimate, closely acquainted; familiar, close.
ex: All my inward friends abhorred me.
He had had occasion, by one very inward with him, to know in part the discourse of his life.

s.def: Devoted to spiritual matters, pious, devout.
Tame.

ety: Etymology tree English inward Middle English -ly English -ly English inwardly From inward + -ly.

s.def: In an inward manner; to or toward the inside or to oneself.
ex: Jacob groaned inwardly when he was called on to answer the question.

s.def: Completely, fully.

ety: From Middle English inwardnesse; analysable as inward + -ness.

s.def: The characteristic of being inward or directed towards the inside.
The internal or true state; the essential nature.
ex: the inwardness of conduct
Sense cannot arrive at th’inwardness of things.

s.def: Familiarity; intimacy.
Earnestness; heartiness.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Germanic *in Proto-West Germanic *in Old English in Middle English in English in English -wards English inwards From in + -wards.

s.def: The third-person singular neuter personal pronoun used to refer to an inanimate object, abstract entity, or non-human living thing.
ex: Take this book and put it on the shelf.
Take each day as it comes.
I found a poor little cat. It seems to be half starving.

s.def: The person who chases and tries to catch the other players in the playground game of tag.
ex: In the next game, Adam and Tom will be it…
Tag, you're it!
When there are only two children left who haven't been tagged, I will stop the game, and we will start over with those children starting as the Its.

s.def: A third-person singular personal pronoun used to refer to a baby or child, especially of unknown gender.
ex: She took the baby and held it in her arms.
The sky was dripping. Like a tap that a child has tried its hardest to turn off but hasn't quite managed.

s.def: A third-person singular pronoun used to refer to an unspecified person.
ex: She had never seen that each human being was different, would react differently, had its own peculiar idiosyncrasies.

s.def: An affectionate third-person singular personal pronoun.
A third-person singular personal pronoun used to refer to an animate referent who is transgender or non-binary.
Refers to someone being identified, often on the phone, but not limited to this situation.
ex: It's me, John.
Somebody wanted a drink, didn't they? Who was it?
It is I, your king.

s.def: The impersonal pronoun, used without referent as the subject of an impersonal verb or statement (known as the dummy pronoun, dummy it or weather it).
ex: It is nearly 10 o’clock.
It’s very cold today.
It’s lonely here without you.

s.def: The impersonal pronoun, used without referent, or with unstated but contextually implied referent, in various short idioms or expressions.
ex: stick it out

s.def: Sex appeal, especially that which goes beyond physical appearance.
ex: 'Tisn't beauty, so to speak, nor good talk necessarily. It's just It. Some women'll stay in a man's memory if they once walked down a street
And she had It. It, hell; she had Those.

s.def: It is inevitable. There is no alternative.
Used to indicate that different situations may produce different results.
ex: As with any builder asked to quote for a house extension, there will be an intake of breath before you're told: "It depends."

s.def: It is not important; do not worry (used to reassure or comfort the person to whom it is said).
ex: I’m afraid I’ve broken your mug. – It doesn’t matter; it was old and I was going to throw it away anyway.

s.def: I withdraw my previous statement (often used if it wasn't heard or understood).
ex: Maybe we could try fixing this part to the … no, wait, it doesn’t matter.

s.def: Said to compliment a meal after eating it.

ety: First quoted as it was Greek to me in Julius Caesar by Shakespeare, possibly translated from a sentence in Medieval Latin.

s.def: I don't understand any of it; it makes no sense.
ex: I tried reading the instructions, but it’s all Greek to me.
"Well," said Alfred, "it may be a letter, but I confess it is all Greek to me. I certainly do not see why you wish to keep it a secret. Tell me."
“It's more like some firm's paper. All this printed stuff at the top. Drachenflieger. Drachenballons. Ballonstoffe. Kugelballons. Greek to me.”

s.def: Indicates that the current situation is an emergency.
Indicates that the weather is cold.
Indicates that rain is falling.
Snow is falling.
Indicates the speaker thinks that the price is too high.

ety: Named after the nation of Italy, as it was first used by an Italian printer, Aldo Manuzio, around 1500. Literally Italy + -ic.

s.def: Designed to resemble a handwriting style developed in Italy in the 16th century.
Having letters that slant or lean to the right; oblique.
ex: The text was impossible to read: every other word was underlined or in a bold or italic font.

s.def: A typeface in which the letters slant to the right.
ex: Names of vessels, as the Kearsarge or the Alabama, are frequently put in italic.
[…] ROBERT GRANJON, possibly in collaboration with CLAUDE GARAMOND, had created an italic which matched Garamond Roman.

s.def: An oblique handwriting style, such as used by Italian calligraphers of the Renaissance.
ex: Spenser uses two different scripts: an Elizabethan secretary hand for English texts, and an italic 'mixed' with secretary graphs for Latin texts […]

ety: Etymology tree English italic Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English italicize From italic + -ize.

s.def: To put into italics.
To emphasize.

ety: From Middle English icche, ȝicche, from Old English ġiċċe (“itch”), from Proto-Germanic *jukjǭ (“itch”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Scots yeuk (“itch, itchiness”), Dutch jeuk (“itch”), German jucken.

s.def: A sensation felt on an area of the skin that causes a person or animal to want to scratch said area.
A constant teasing desire or want.
To feel itchy; to feel a need to be scratched.
To have a constant, teasing urge; to feel strongly motivated; to want or desire something.
ex: He started learning to drive and he has been itching for opportunities to practice ever since.

s.def: To cause to feel an itch.
ex: My head is suddenly itching me like mad.

s.def: To scratch or rub so as to relieve an itch.
ex: "What makes you suspect him?" Max asked as he itched his neck.
I have to take both shoes and socks off! If I go bare foot I'm ok! I also get itching on my r/palm of my hand. I itch it so much that it's raw!
Ulysses thumped his side and itched his back side, then slipped into his car.

s.def: Sarcoptes scabiei, a parasitic arthropod that burrows into the skin and causes scabies.

ety: From Middle English item, from Latin item (“also; in the same manner”). The present English meaning derives from a usage in lists, where the first entry would begin in primis (“firstly”) or imprimis, and the other entries with item (“also, moreover”). Later, the members of lists were referred to as "items".

s.def: An object that can be picked up for later use.
A distinct physical object.
ex: Tweezers are great for manipulating small items.

s.def: A line of text having a legal or other meaning; a separate particular in an account.
ex: the items in a bill
In response to the first item, we deny all wrongdoing.
Beyond being mere items of a legal code, they [the mitzvot] are the very basis of the relationship that God and the people Israel have established.

s.def: A question on a test, which may include its answers.
ex: The exam has 100 items, each of which includes a correct response and three distractors.

s.def: A matter for discussion in an agenda.
ex: The first item for discussion is the budget for next year's picnic.

s.def: Two people who are having a romantic or sexual relationship with each other.
ex: Jack and Jill are an item.
Are we an item? Girl, quit playin' / "We're just friends," what are you sayin'?

s.def: A short article in a newspaper.
ex: an item concerning the weather

s.def: A hint; an innuendo.
ex: A secret item was given to some of the bishops […] to absent themselves.

s.def: Ellipsis of item girl.
To make a note of.

ety: The adjective is first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1533, the noun in 1941; partly inherited from Middle English iterat(e) (adjective), partly borrowed from Latin iterātus, perfect passive participle of iterō (“to do something for a second time, repeat”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)) , from iterum (“again”) + -ō. Sporadical participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

s.def: To perform or repeat an action on each item in a set.
ex: The max() function iterates through the data to find the highest value.

s.def: To perform or repeat an action on the results of each such prior action.
ex: In mathematics, an iterated function is a function which is composed with itself, possibly ad infinitum, in a process called iteration.

s.def: To utter or do a second time or many times; to repeat.
ex: to iterate advice
Nor Eve to iterate / Her former trespass feared.

s.def: To repeat an activity, making incremental changes each time.
An n-fold self-composition of a function.
The image of a certain value under such a function.
ex: f²(x₀) is the second iterate of x₀ under f.

s.def: Said or done again; repeated.
Iterated.

ety: From Late Latin itinerantem, present active participle of itineror (“travel”), from itiner-. By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ant.

s.def: Habitually travelling from place to place.
ex: an itinerant preacher or peddler

s.def: One who travels from place to place.
A member of the Travelling Community, whether settled or not.

ety: From Middle English itinerarie, from Latin itinerārium (“an account of a journey, a road-book”), from iter (“a way, journey”). By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ary.

s.def: A route or proposed route of a journey.
An account or record of a journey.
A guidebook for travellers.
A written schedule of activities for a vacation or road trip.
Itinerant; travelling from place to place; done on a journey.
ex: It were rather an itinerary circuit of justice than a progress.

ety: By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ate.

s.def: To travel from place to place, especially to preach or lecture.

ety: Equivalent to it + -s (possessive marker). From the earlier form it's (it + -'s), which is now considered nonstandard. Began to displace his as the possessive of the neuter pronoun in the Middle English period; had fully displaced it by the 1700s.

s.def: Belonging to it.
ex: The manner wherewith our Lawes assay to moderate the foolish and vaine expences of table-cheare and apparell, seemeth contrarie to it's end.
since I have been at the Pains to write it, if he consents to it's being published I will follow my Friend's Advice, and chiefly yours.
The Chinese government is at war with its own people.

s.def: The one (or ones) belonging to it.
ex: … both Houses have resolved to rob the North of a good friend of its and yours.
EBay Canada argued in court that the data sought by tax collectors was not its to give.

s.def: Obsolete spelling of it's.
plural of it

ety: From Middle English hit-self, equivalent to it + -self.

s.def: it; A thing as the object of a verb or preposition that also appears as the subject
ex: When the opportunity presented itself, no feasible course of action suggested itself (to us).

s.def: it; used to intensify the subject, especially to emphasize that it is the only participant in the predicate
ex: The door itself is quite heavy.

s.def: it; used to refer back to an earlier subject
ex: The oil by degrees gets covered with a curdy mass, which after some time settles to the bottom, while itself becomes limpid and colorless.

ety: From Middle English yvory, ivorie, from Anglo-Norman ivurie, from Latin eboreus (“in or of ivory”) adjective of ebur (“ivory”) (genitive eboris), from Demotic Egyptian yb (“ivory, Elephantine”) (compare Coptic ⲓⲏⲃ (iēb, “Elephantine”)), from Egyptian ꜣbw (“elephant, ivory, Elephantine”), from Proto-Afroasiatic *leb-. Displaced native Old English elpendbān (literally “elephant bone”).

s.def: material
The hard white form of dentin which forms the tusks of elephants, walruses and other animals.
A creamy white color, the color of ivory.
Something made from or resembling ivory.
The teeth.
ex: Ye forgot some o' yer ivories, didn't ye, on th' grass?

s.def: The keys of a piano; or, the white keys, as opposed to the black keys (ebonies).
ex: to tickle the ivories
Tony had gone into the storage room and gotten two more standing lamps, one placed near the ebonies and ivories.

s.def: A white person.
A die (object bearing numbers, thrown in games of chance).
Made of ivory.
Resembling or having the colour of ivory.
ex: The walls and ceiling of this drawing-room in Montague Square are painted ivory.

ety: Calque of French tour d'ivoire, based on a biblical phrase, coined by Charles Augustin Sainte-Beuve to compare the poet Alfred de Vigny (more isolated) with Victor Hugo (more socially engaged). First attested in English in a translation of Laughter by French philosopher Henri Bergson (1911). The term was popularized in The Ivory Tower (1917) by Henry James, though used in different sense (millionaires, not professors).

s.def: A sheltered, overly-academic existence or perspective, implying a disconnection or lack of awareness of reality or practical considerations.
ex: Such a proposal looks fine from an ivory tower, but it could never work in real life.

ety: From Middle English ivi, from Old English īfiġ, from Proto-West Germanic *ibig, *ibag, *ibah, from Proto-Germanic *ibahs (compare West Flemish iefte, Low German Eiloov, Ieloof, German Efeu), from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)ebʰ- (compare Welsh efwr (“black elder”), Ancient Greek ἴφυον (íphuon, “spike-lavender, Lavandula Spica”)).

s.def: Any of several woody, climbing, or trailing evergreen plants of the genus Hedera.
Any similar plant of any genus.
